en: Salutation to Śrī Sundaragaṇapati.
[Commentary on the Varuṇapaddhati] (F 1 is blank)
I pay homage to the auspicious Kalpaka-Vināyaka, who is crowded with greedy bees hovering over the flow of ichor constantly streaming from his broad temples.
I take refuge at the lotus feet of the Dancing King, the Lord of Actors, who bestows the joy of raising up Vyāghrapāda’s hands in salutation as he dances;
[those feet] which delight the Lord of Actors with the playful movements of their own tender limbs.
May the goddess Śivakāmapriyā grant eternal auspiciousness.
Having paid homage to the Guru and the Goddess of Speech,
this eye of the virtuous is ever opened by means of the illustrious *Varuṇapaddhati*.
The brief elucidation of this [text] spoken by Śiva has been declared by my gurus;
following that, I shall speak it concisely and logically according to my capacity.

Then the preceptor named Varuṇa, whose mind was purified by the thorough knowledge of the many secrets of the Śiva-āgamas, [taught] with the desire to favor all people the initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is the seed and the essential core of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Desiring to speak, [the author] first pays homage to his chosen deity and declares his intention to undertake the work in order to fulfill the traditional conduct of the learned:
"Salutation to Tripurasundarī."
Homage to Soma, the source of bliss, who possesses the seeds of the two types of nirvāṇa;
now, the two seed-syllables for initiation and consecration are being collected.

For the sake of the two seeds of *nirvāṇa*—which serve as the cause for the pair of ultimate goals (*niḥśreyasa*) characterized by the departure from the bonds of impurity and so forth—the suffix *dvā* is applied to the root *dvi*, according to the rule "the roots *nis* and *pūrva-dvā-gati-gandhana*" take *dvā*. Liberation (*mukti*) is [defined as] *kaivalya*, *nirvāṇa*, *śreyaḥ*, *niḥśreyasa*, and *amṛta*. It is the cause; it is the cause, the reason, the instrument, and the seed.
The chowrie. To the question "What is the cause of this?", he says:
"To Soma," that is, to him who is accompanied by Umā. Here, by the word "Umā," the Śakti who is intent upon bestowing grace is intended; [the offering is] precisely for him who is accompanied by her.

Because it is the cause for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), that power (*śakti*)—being twofold through the distinction between being without a substratum (*niradhikaraṇa*) and having a substratum (*sādhikaraṇa*)—becomes the cause of the two kinds of *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, it is stated that there are two kinds of *nirvāṇa* precisely because of this twofold nature of grace (*anugraha*). For this very reason, Śambhu says:

"Śambhu is he from whom liberation arises in this way; to that Śiva, [I offer] salutation. By this, it is indicated that he alone is worthy of salutation and no other, because no one else possesses the quality of being the uprooter of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
As it has been said:

"Those who, abandoning the Lord Īśāna with Ambā, worship other [deities] for the sake of liberation, they are overcome by great darkness; for them there is no supreme goal. Those who, abandoning the Lord Īśāna with Ambā, worship another deity, fall into the most terrible saṃsāra, utterly deluded. Now, following the salutation to one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā):
By this, at the beginning of the treatise, it is indicated that the salutation to the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and the necessity of the *ga* syllable are essential;
otherwise, the word *dha* would have been used at the very beginning of the verse. [This is because] between the two terms *dīkṣā* and *pratiṣṭhā*, by the word *dīkṣā*...

The "hungry ghosts" (kṣudhādayaḥ) and so forth to be mentioned [in the fourth line] refer to the *pratiṣṭhā* [deities], while the "immobile beings" (sthāvarādayaḥ) and so forth refer to those yet to be mentioned. The two seeds (*bīja*) for both of these are the cause of *nirvāṇa*;
the meaning is that they are the *pratiṣṭhās* and the *dānas*. Alternatively, it may be understood that what is included here is that which motivates activity in both cases.

Because [the teachings] are very extensive in the Āgamas, they are summarized by us for the sake of easily grasping the essential meaning; this is the remainder of the sentence. By this statement, it is expressed that because this [text] is the root, it requires no further dependence. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the seed of the two types of Nirvāṇa," some say as follows:

When consciousness has attained isolation (*vijñānakaivalya*), there is for them one Nirvāṇa characterized by the cessation of *prakṛti’s* authority, which is synonymous with the supreme attainment of powers such as *aṇimā*; this is because, for those who have transcended karma, only the impurity (*mala*) remains in the form of *māyā*. However, another [type of Nirvāṇa] is preceded by the bondage and liberation from *adhikāra*.

Others, however, maintain that it is the direct manifestation of the state of Śiva. Indeed, initiation alone is the singular liberation; just as, for example, in the case of a boy who has been initiated, even though his body remains exactly as it was before, [he attains it] by the power of the scripture.

By means of the sacrament known as *upanayana*, a second birth is accepted. Likewise here too, through initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); however, his manifestation of the state of Śiva occurs after the fall of the body.

Others, however, based on the sequence of the two-fold nature of the womb (*yoni*), state that there are two kinds of *nirvāṇa*. Indeed, for men, [the womb] is twofold: consisting of one's own mother and consisting of the material cause of the universe. It is heard [in scripture]: "the womb...
(2nd line).
"One presides over the womb. Therefore, there is only one final birth to be attained, which is Nirvāṇa, because after that there is no further birth for him.
Furthermore, although the womb is the source of the universe, it is also the manifestation of Śiva-nature; thus, due to the absence of succession, it is twofold.

Regarding the term "nirvāṇa," even within these three positions, because it would entail the attainment of enjoyment (bhukti), it would not be a bond for the sake of liberation; for the contradiction characterized by the non-coexistence of enjoyment and liberation is difficult to avoid.
Now, in accordance with the order of the enumeration, he states the definition and the cause of initiation (dīkṣā) in order to explain it first.

(4th line) That action by which the state of Śiva is manifested through the specific removal of the three bonds is called initiation (*dīkṣā*), characterized by devotion and dispassion. By that action, [he removes] the three bonds: *mala* and *māyā*.

The state of Śiva, which is already present within the self but obscured by impurity (mala), is manifested— just like Śiva himself— in the form of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth, accompanied by the cessation of the bondage of the three fetters consisting of karma and physical form.

It is manifested. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is characterized by devotion (*bhakti*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). Devotion to Śiva is eightfold or ninefold; as it is stated in the *Śivadharmottara*: "The Lord [possesses] affection for His devotees and rejoices in their worship."
Personal worship of Me, performing bodily gestures for My sake, devotion upon hearing My stories,
and the transformation of one's voice, eyes, and limbs [through emotion],
as well as constant remembrance of Me— this is for one who worships Me.

He lives [in truth]. Indeed, he in whom this eightfold devotion exists—even if he is a mere slave—is a lord among Brahmins, a glorious sage, an ascetic, and a scholar. In some places, it is said to be ninefold;
namely: hearing, chanting, remembering Śambhu, washing his feet, worshiping, bowing, serving, and friendship. (f2.b)
And the offering. Thus, the ninefold devotion has been proclaimed by the Lord Śambhu. [It leads to] detachment from saṃsāra.

Because it is the object of the desire to abandon existence produced by birth, which possesses the tree of endless births and deaths, it is to be rejected (*heyatva*). Both [definitions] characterize and make known [the subject], thus it is called a *lakṣaṇa* (definition).
The meaning is that it is the primary cause (*nidāna*) that sets [the process] in motion. By this, [it is shown that] only those possessed of devotion and dispassion [are eligible] for initiation.
The qualification [for initiation]. And the root cause of those two is precisely the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*), and its function is the state of equilibrium (*sāmya*).
As it has been said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
For those embodied beings whose power falls even toward cessation,
their indicative mark is a longing for liberation and an aversion to worldly existence.
Likewise, in the Vāmadeva [Tantra]:
"The teacher deserves to bestow grace upon the disciple in accordance with the descent of power (*śaktipāta*);
where power has not descended, there purification does not arise."
There is no knowledge, no auspicious conduct, no liberation, and no supernatural powers;
therefore, one must repeatedly observe the signs of the descent of power (śaktipāta).

The Guru should purify the disciple either through knowledge or through ritual action. In the *Kiraṇatantra*: "Indeed, the timing of that descent [of power] is equal to the [spiritual] work performed."

"The time of an action is equal, whether it be a moment or something equivalent"— thus, when there is a connection of deficiency or excess through action, confusion indeed arises regarding enjoyments. The absence of that [confusion] results from the attainment of power (*śakti*), and that occurs solely by the power of time.
That too has been stated:
"In that very case, because of the relationship between the excessive and the deficient, confusion arises; for the excessive [power] attains its capacity through the absence of deficiency."

Due to the connection with beginningless seeds, Śiva depends upon time; time is said to be manifold, and the Lord Śiva is the knower of that. Just as someone, when aiming at a moving target, depends upon a certain duration of time, so too does that Śiva [act] simultaneously with the knower of it.
"It depends. Thus, the connection that "this action is initiation" (*dīkṣā*) is what is called the *saṃdhi* (junction).

And so, the meaning of *dīkṣā* is: because it bestows the manifestation of the self's nature as Śiva, and because it destroys the bondage of the fetters (*pāśa*). As it has been said: "Knowledge is given (*dīyate*), and [the state of being bound] is destroyed (*kṣīyate*)."
"The accumulation of bonds is given away and exhausted through yoga; this is what is here called the word 'initiation' (dīkṣā). And thus:
Since that [action] does not bestow both fruits upon another action, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
It is not the case that "the two fruits belong to her" merely because she has proceeded according to the varying degrees of the descent of power (*śakti*).

And there is non-pervasion. Having thus stated the definition of initiation (*dīkṣā*), he speaks of the vision of one who has been initiated [in the fourth line] in order to state the definition of the bound soul (*paśu*) which is the cause for its occurrence: "Therefore, knowledge, devotion, and detachment... and so forth.

These are the signs of the self who is initiated; however, they do not apply directly to the sacrificial animal. Since initiation is characterized by dispassion (*vairāgya*), therefore knowledge is Śiva himself, the All.

"Supreme," "the liberator from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu)," "knowledge," "devotion to Śiva," and "dispassion toward saṃsāra"— this triad is the set of signs and characteristics of the self that has been initiated, manifesting here in this very life.
As it has been said in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"Discrimination arises from knowledge regarding things that are to be abandoned and things that are to be adopted."
One who is dispassionate toward the cycle of existence that is to be abandoned seeks that which is to be accepted.

Having recognized Śiva as that which is to be accepted, one then practices devotion toward Him; and one seeks a Guru who is a proponent of the path of devotion. Initiated by the Guru, who is Śiva himself, through mantras and initiation, the bound soul (paśu) becomes liberated from saṃsāra.
Likewise, in the Pauṣkara [Tantra]:
"Detachment quickly arises from the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra:
'When shall I see the Lord of Gods? When shall I be released from bondage?'"
Or who indeed is the one who reveals Śambhu? Such is the thought that arises;
for thus does the Lord bestow grace upon one from all sides within the cycle of transmigration.
[Objection: But surely devotion, knowledge, and dispassion can arise even for one who has not been initiated, by virtue of meritorious deeds performed in previous lives.
To this, he says: "of the bound soul" (paśoḥ). These qualities—devotion and the rest—belong to the bound soul who is uninitiated.
The essential truths come into being; although they may arise by virtue of meritorious deeds performed in previous births, even those are as flickering as the light of a lamp.

However, for one who is initiated, by the power of the compassionate glance of a Guru who possesses the weight of the Śiva-nature, they become like a diamond pillar—this is the meaning. But in truth, you are not merely [those] essential [truths].

"Amarasiṃha states that these two [are the characteristics]. However, since it was said that for the bound soul (paśu), these do not apply directly, [the author] now states the definition of the bound soul (paśu-lakṣaṇa) in order to make it known that initiation (dīkṣā) alone is the cause even for the characteristics of the bound soul and its fetters (pāśa)."

The *paśu* (bound soul) is one who knows only a little (*kiñcijña*), is impure (*malina*), is divided (*bhinna*), is an agent (*kartṛ*) and an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) by virtue of its own karma, is possessed of a body (*śarīrāḍhya*), is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), is eternally conditioned (*nityasaṃskārya*), and is without lordship (*anīśvara*). It is called *kiñcijña* because it knows only a little; however, there is no omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) for the state of the liberated (*mukta*). Therefore, knowing only a little is indeed the characteristic of the *paśu*.

The characteristic [of the Lord] is defined by this much alone: that he is distinguished from the fettered (paśu) by his being the Lord (pati). This is because the Lord is omniscient, whereas the fetter is ignorant.

As for others [the individual souls], they say that [their distinction] is precisely through the attribute that establishes their limited knowledge (kiñcijjñatva). For this very reason, [the soul] is "impure" due to the bond of beginningless impurity (anādimala-bandha).
As it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"Due to the connection with beginningless impurity, the state of being sullied resides in the individual soul (*aṇu*);
due to the liberation from beginningless impurity, the state of being stainless resides in Śiva."
Therefore, it is "distinct," meaning differentiated from the Lord; the sense is that the individual soul (jīva) is not the Lord himself.

He states the cause for its impurity: it is the "agent and experiencer of its own actions," namely merit and demerit, and is thus dependent upon them—this is the sense. Regarding experience, by the word "action" (karman), [the latent impressions of action are meant].

Pleasure, pain, and so forth are mentioned. By their own specific terms, the fixed nature of the objects of experience is stated. And regarding experience, he states the means: "the body and so forth. (f4.a, 1st line)

That deluded soul is endowed with various bodies corresponding to its respective actions; otherwise, the occurrence of those various diverse enjoyments would be impossible. Now, one might ask: since that which is endowed with a body is limited and non-eternal, how can it be the enjoyer of the fruits of action in other places or in other births? To this, he says: "It is all-pervading and eternal. (2nd)

The meaning of "all-pervading" (*vibhu*) is that it is omnipresent and complete; it is devoid of non-existence throughout the three periods of time. It is "all-pervading" because it is the cause of experiencing [objects] in other locations. [This applies to] another birth...
The cause of future enjoyment is "eternal"; otherwise, there would result a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*) between the enjoyment and its causes.

Now, one might ask: since objects of enjoyment (*bhoga*) are insentient by nature, and since this [individual soul] possesses only limited knowledge and is impure, how can there be a fixed determination of objects within those enjoyments? To this he says: "together with the Lord" (*seśvara*), meaning accompanied by the Lord; that is, dependent upon the Lord.
The meaning is as follows. It is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"O twice-born sage, it is because this living being is ignorant that he is not his own master."
That too would exist only through dependence, like a jar or other objects in its own manifestation.
How can he be accepted as the agent? Therefore, Maheśvara is the agent. This is the characteristic of the bound soul (*paśu*).

It has been explained in detail in the *Śataratnasaṃgrahavyākhyāna* (line 5); it is not elaborated here. And thus, because actions are impermanent, their fruit exists in another place and at another time.

To the question "How is there the state of being an enjoyer?", he says: "He is to be refined" (*saṃskāryaḥ*). "Refinement" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the residual trace of past actions (*karman*) produced by defilement, or that which is fit for the refinement of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
This very one is called the "bound soul" (*paśu*). And this general definition of the bound soul applies to both the *vijñānākala* and the *pralayākala*.
The specific characteristics of the three types of fettered souls (*paśu*), including those of all forms, will be explained later.
And so it is stated in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The soul is a fettered being, yet it is autonomous, consisting of pure consciousness, and defiled by impurities."
"Confused, eternally transmigrating, possessing only limited knowledge, devoid of sovereignty, and inactive"—

having thus stated the characteristics of the bound soul (*paśu*), he now states the characteristics of the fetters (*pāśa*) in order to indicate that, although the triad of fetters beginning with *mala* is to be purified during initiation (*dīkṣā*), it is nevertheless the [impurity] that impels even that [limited] knowledge. (f4.b1st)

The fetters (pāśas) are also to be known as threefold: impurity (mala), Māyā, and Karma. Among these, impurity (mala) is mentioned first because it is the primary fetter for the three [classes of souls]: the Vijñānakalas and the Pralayākalas.

Immediately after [the mention of] *māyā*, because both [categories] distinct from the *vijñānakala* are bonds (*pāśa*), and because *sakala* alone is the bond of *māyā*, [the text] subsequently mentions *karman*. Here, it defiles (*malinīkaroti*).
The impurity (*mala*) is that which conceals the self’s own inherent knowledge, action, and will; furthermore, it is indeed beginningless.
As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "Now, the impurity of persons is beginningless. This [impurity] constitutes the meaning of the term "bond" (*pāśa*).

Even in the state of being an animal (*paśutva*), there is inclusion [of consciousness]; for without that, the very state of being an animal would not exist. Thus it has been said: "An animal [is so called] due to its conjunction with the state of being an animal. Now, one might object: consciousness consists of the nature of vision and action, and since that exists in the self at all times—as seen in the case of the Lord of Elephants (*mugendra*) and others—is he not therefore omniscient?

It is established that the state of Śiva—consisting of agency, consciousness, and so forth—exists eternally even within the self (ātman). Furthermore, because impurity (mala) is beginningless, the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) associated with it is also established. Therefore, how can these two exist in mutual exclusion?

If it is asked how the states of being Śiva and being a bound soul (paśu) can reside in a single self— being like light and darkness— the answer is true: although the self's nature as Śiva, characterized by omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth, is established from beginningless time, it remains obscured because it has been defiled by beginningless impurity (mala).

Because its capacity to grasp its own object—namely, the yellowness of gold covered by the blackness of a mirage—is obstructed, it remains internalized within itself; however, it does not perish in its own nature, nor does it become insentient within itself. And if this were so, [it would be like] the eternity, omnipresence, and other qualities of the self.
It should not be argued that the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*)— being defiled by beginningless impurity— is likewise subject to cessation;
for just as the nature of gold is manifested when ore is processed with mercury, the manifestation of the state of Śiva is logically established even for one whose self has attained knowledge.
As it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*: "Just as copper, when processed with mercury,
attains the state of gold, so too the self, when permeated by knowledge, attains the state of Śiva."

In this context, "endowed with knowledge" (jñānasambhinna) means one who is joined with the activity of the Guru— who is Śiva in form— known as initiation (dīkṣā), which manifests all-encompassing knowledge in the sense that "by this, everything is known. Just as the cataract of the eye is removed by the action of a physician, so too is the [impurity] of the Self [removed] by initiation.
For this very reason, the injunction regarding cessation is established solely through the operation of the Lord.
Then, for the sake of manifesting liberation from the bonds of karma— known as the impurity of the self and māyā— and for the manifestation of the state of Śiva-ness,
knowledge proceeds forth from Śiva.

For this very reason, the teachers have provided the following explanation right there in that same [text] regarding the statement of Svāyambhuva: "Initiation proceeds from Śiva. It has indeed been stated: "Initiation alone liberates; it leads one upward even to the abode of Śiva. Now, an objection might be raised: since initiation is an action (*karman*), it must be binding, just like the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and others.
If it is argued that [the teacher] would thus not be the cause of liberation, that is true.
Just as a snake-charmer (jāṅgalika) effects the removal of poison through the power of mantras and rituals such as meditation,
so too does the teacher effect the disentanglement from the bonds (pāśa) of impurity and the like solely through the ritual act of initiation (dīkṣā), which is empowered by the power of Śiva.
Śiva indeed brings about manifestation as well;
and thus it has been stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
Just as one effects the removal of poison through the power of meditative seeds (*dhyānabīja*),
so too does the Noble One effect the severance of the noose through the sacrifices to Śiva.
And furthermore:

It is heard in scripture that through rites such as expiation (*prāyaścitta*), there is liberation from evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*); likewise here too, there is liberation from the bonds (*pāśa*), so there is no contradiction. But surely, because impurity (*mala*) is beginningless and is admitted to be eternal, its nature as an obscuration of the Self is self-evident, just like the heat of fire.

And thus, only through the destruction of impurity (*mala*) is the destruction of its state as an obscuration possible. However, the cessation of the binding nature of the fetters (*pāśas*) such as *mala* is indeed like the death of a poisonous tumor (*viṣagranthi*).

It is performed by means of initiation (*dīkṣā*), just as the cessation of the power of ignorance (*katva-śakti*) is brought about; thus there is no contradiction. Since impurity (*mala*) is insentient (*jaḍa*) and manifold, it would follow that objects such as jars would be non-eternal. Therefore, its unity alone must be accepted.
And this being so, when that [impurity] is suppressed for the sake of the single liberation of one [soul], [all are liberated].

If it is argued that this would entail universal liberation [for all souls], we say no; for although impurity (*mala*) is unitary, the soul is accepted as possessing multiple powers. And thus it has been said:
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*,
it is stated that the individual soul (*āṇava*)— which resides within each person, possesses its own power of limitation until the end of time,
and contains a multitude of powers— is indeed of a single nature, yet likewise endowed with diverse powers. (3rd verse)
Like the blackness in copper, that too is innate and does not enter from without;
just as the husk and the bran are innate to the grain of rice.

It is said that "inborn impurity" (*sahaja-mala*) is thus [the cause]; and since the cessation of that [impurity] occurs through a single descent of power (*śaktipāta*), it is established that liberation belongs only to one whose [impurity] has been restrained at that time, and not to any other—enough of this elaboration. The reality that is the cause of the world of *māyā* is eternal, and not...
Its form is false, like that of the Vedāntins. As it is said in the *Tattvaprakāśa*:
"Māyā is a real entity, the root of the universe, and eternal; karma consists of dharma and adharma."
It is established by the Vedas; it is so stated because it is to be understood solely through the Vedas,
as [stated] in the *Svāyambhuva*.

The comprehension of the *dharmaśāstra* arises from the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) alone. He states the definition according to the enumeration: "Impurity" (*mala*) is impurity (*aśuddhi*), which is ignorance (*ajñāna*); it obstructs consciousness (*caitanya*). Such is the definition of impurity; and it is that [impurity].
Impurity (*aśuddhi*). To the question "Of what kind is it?", he says: "Ignorance" (*ajñāna*), which means the opposite of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Since the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) here is opposition—among its meanings being non-existence, opposition, and difference—he states this very point for that reason.

The meaning is that it obstructs the consciousness of the Self and obstructs its innate qualities, such as omniscience. He describes the nature of *māyā* by way of its effects: "The aggregate of principles (*tattvasaṃhati*) consists of everything from *māyā*, *kalā*, and so forth, down to earth."
That from which the collection of principles— from Time down to Earth—
arises, that is the aggregate of principles; she from whose presence the existence of these occurs is Māyā, Kalā, and so forth.
The meaning is that *māyā* is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the principles ending with earth. Now, he states the definition of action (*karman*).
This action, consisting of both dharma and adharma, is clearly evident.

To the question of to whom these three bonds belong, he says: "Because by these bonds the *paśu* [is bound]"; that is, by these bonds—namely, for some by *mala* alone, and for others by all three: *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman*.

The meaning is that by being bound [by these], one attains the state of a *paśu* (bound soul). Thus, it is indicated that the essential definition of being a *paśu* is precisely the state of being bound by fetters (*pāśabandhatva*). This demonstrates the effect of these three fetters upon the *paśu*.

Due to the ignorance of the bound soul (*paśu*), there is a connection with *māyā* for the sake of experiencing the fruits of actions. Because of the bound soul’s ignorance—that is, because its consciousness is veiled by the impurity of experience—there is a connection with *māyā*;

the meaning is that this consists precisely in the relationship with the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with *pṛthivī*, which is indeed the connection with the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*). [This pertains to] the actions...
For the sake of experience, she becomes the source of pleasure and pain; this is the remainder [of the passage] from the *Svāyambhuva*.

In the determination that experience for this person consisting of consciousness is the momentary sensation of pleasure, pain, and so forth, the teacher Jyotirācārya has established that this [person] is bound by the collection of principles beginning with earth and ending with time. Furthermore, it is said that this [person], like a spider, wanders through all the bodies born within the worlds due to its karma.
And in the *Śrīmanmṛgendra*, it is stated: "This [term] establishes its literal meaning from the agent (*prayoktṛ*) down to the great earth (*mahī*).
This is according to the *Pauṣkara*.
"Each [element] is determined by the male [organ], ending with time and the king.
Thus [it is said].
In the *Tattvaprakāśa* it is also said:
"Endowed with the body of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*), [the soul] shall exist within all wombs by the power of karma."
"The city of eight" refers to the internal instruments and the external instruments of action. Now, in the venerable *Kālottara*, it is said:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell constitute the pentad."
"The intellect, the mind, and the ego—this is declared to be the 'city of eight' (puryaṣṭaka). Thus it is heard in scripture.
If it is asked, "How then can [the body] consist of the principles (tattva) beginning with Time and ending with Earth?"— this is true,
as was stated by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha on the occasion of commenting upon the Sūtra; there, in accordance with the *Mṛgendra*, he explained it precisely as being comprised of thirty principles.

This has been explained. In response to the inquiry as to how this [self] possesses the nature of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), [the answer is: the elements (*bhūta*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*)—[and so forth].

There is no contradiction, according to Aghoraśivācārya, because that [body] is composed of five groups known as the organs of action and the internal organ; its cause, which is the *pradhāna*—which possesses the nature of those qualities (*guṇas*) and supplies them; and the triad consisting of the *kañcukas* beginning with *kalā*, which assist the essential nature of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Thus, there is no inconsistency.
This has been refuted. Now, one might ask: "If this is so, how can there be experience for this self, which is bound by the three bonds beginning with *anādi*?
To this, he says:

Liberation occurs by the will of the Lord through initiation and so forth; otherwise, it would not. Therefore, one enjoys the entirety of pleasure and other experiences according to one's own karma. "Of this bound soul (paśu), initiation is the beginning" refers to that which is called initiation, which is preceded by the will of the Lord. It is precisely from that [initiation]...

Liberation occurs for the sake of initiation (*dīkṣā*) designated as the "special nirvāṇa" (*viśeṣanirvāṇa*); the remainder [of the sentence] is that there is the release from the three bonds (*pāśatraya*).
Otherwise, it simply does not occur by means of another method established in other scriptures (*śāstrāntara*), because of that reason.

Let it be that for those liberated according to other scriptures, liberation consists in the attainment of various levels of reality (tattvas) subordinate to the principle of Śiva; yet because such liberation is characterized by gradation,
involves return [to worldly existence], and lacks the release from the bondage of the three fetters (pāśatraya), it does not constitute true liberation for this [system].

Its correspondence with reality [is established] because it consists in the attainment of the state of Śiva, which is supreme among all; because it is free from rebirth; and because its primary aim is liberation from the bondage of the three fetters (pāśas).
As it has been said: "The Cārvākas, the Kaulikas, and those who know the science of astrology are merely materialists."

(4th line) The Sāṃkhyas [hold that] the eye and other sense organs are established as consisting of those [subtle elements] alone; others [the Vaiśeṣikas] hold they are composed of earth and so forth; the Naiyāyikas [hold they are composed of] the quality of egoity.

The Buddhists abide in the principle of intellect (*buddhi*), while those established in the qualities of the Buddha abide in the intellect. Those who know the *Pāñcarātra* consider Prakṛti to be Hari; the Vedāntins, the Sāṃkhyas, and the Yogins abide in the Puruṣa.
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"That which is absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) arising from the discrimination between the subject (*puṃs*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), or that which is the cessation [of thought] after considering everything as Brahman—
whatever liberations there may be produced by bonds, they all attain non-difference within the process of emanation."

In the Śaiva Siddhānta, it shines forth that for others [who are not liberated], there is no creation of the unliberated; nor does [the Lord] descend below the level of the individual soul (*puruṣa*).
Having pervaded all things with His own nature, He, the Lord of All, remains eternally established in His pure sovereignty.
(7th line)

Therefore, according to another treatise, because there is no liberation at all, one experiences— that is, undergoes— the enjoyment of all things such as pleasure and pain, which consist of happiness and suffering produced solely by one's own karma, namely by the merits and demerits one has performed oneself. Furthermore, [it is said that] even the liberated one [experiences] the state of being the possessor of the fruit and the fruit itself.
He said: That bound soul is a transmigrating beast (paśu), though it is liberated from the [primary] bond yet remains possessed of the three fetters (pāśatraya).
Due to the bondage of the three fetters, it transmigrates through many births, deaths, pleasures, and pains;
thus, that bound soul is a "transmigrating beast" (saṃsāra-paśu). Because of the binding by the three fetters, it is called "bondage" (bandha).
He who was bound by the three fetters is called "liberated" when he has been released from those three fetters through initiation (dīkṣā).
Likewise, in the *Suprabheda*:
"The self (*ātman*) covered by impurities is called 'bondage' (*paśu*) by the wise;
that same self, when freed from impurities, is called 'liberation' (*mukti*) by the wise."

Now, it is said that through initiation (*dīkṣā*) there is liberation from the three bonds (*pāśatraya*). In this regard, one might raise the doubt as to whether all selves (*ātman*) are bound by the three bonds, or whether some are bound while others are not; anticipating this, he speaks of the "bound soul" (*paśu*) in order to explain that [point] first.
This [bound soul] is to be favored in three ways: as the sakala, the pralayākala, and the vijñānākala; their essential nature will be explained hereafter.

The one to be favored describes the experience of Śiva in the form of initiation (*dīkṣā*). This aforementioned bound soul (*paśu*), who is the object [of grace], is threefold—that is, of three kinds; the singular number is used because they have arisen as a single category. He states those very types: *sakala* (the "with-parts"), who possesses the bond of *kalā*; *pralayākala*, who at the time of dissolution possesses the bond of *kalā*; and *vijñānakala*, by means of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).
"Directly endowed with the power of the knowledge of God along with the bond of *kalā*.
Thus, these [categories] are threefold; since it is not possible to engage in initiation without a thorough knowledge of their characteristics, he promises to state those characteristics. Of these...

Now the definition of essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) is being stated: The *sakala* [individual] is one whose [powers] are severed by *māyā*, *karman*, and *mala*; he who is veiled by *mala* and *karman* is the *pralayākala*.

The connection with the bond of impurity (*malaikabandhasambandha*) is called *vijñānākala*. This knowledge—even the knowledge regarding the distinctions of authority within the various types of initiation (*dīkṣābheda*)—is also the seed of initiation; this is the intended meaning. According to the order of enumeration...
(line 2).
He explains the moment: having reflected thus, [he says] that among them, the first is associated with impurity (*mala*); the second is associated with impurity, *karman*, and *māyā*;
and the *sakala* is that which is bound by beginningless entities through the process of flowing and so forth, and by *karman*.

The *sakala* (the "with-parts" or limited soul) is also so designated because it is endowed with a *kalā*. This term *kalā* indicates that portion of the innate knowledge and agency of the *puruṣa* which manifests upon the partial removal of impurity (*mala*). That very [power] is called *māyā*; thus it is stated in the *Cintyaviśva*: "That indeed is *māyā*... (4th line).
And Manu produced Kalā in due order;

having separated the atom (aṇu), the individual soul (māṇava), and impurity (mala) from one another, and having established them within the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), he manifested the power of agency (kartṛ-śakti). However, by means of the bondage of Kalā, the object [of experience] is not itself of the nature of bondage for the selves.

This is declared to be *kalā* because it is the cause of the experience (*bhoga*) of the *aṇus*. Now, is it not the case that *kalā* is said to be that which manifests the ignorance (*ajñatva*) and agency (*kartṛtva*) of the self?

If it is asked, "Let that [bondage] arise through Śiva’s power alone; what need is there for *kalā*? [we reply: Śiva, however, does not manifest the powers of ignorance (*ajñatva*) and agency (*kartṛtva*) within the self without the *pāśa*.
And as it is stated in the *Tattvasaṅgraha*:
"Just as a snare binds one who is not bound, so too does the fault of unwholesome association [bind] one who is not bound; it is like the power of an agent. (Verse 7th line)

[Objection: "Surely, let that [kalā] exist for the sake of the self's enjoyment alone, for the purpose of manifesting the states of being known and being an agent; let it not be through *karman*, because in the absence of *karman*, there would be no enjoyment for the *vijñāna-kalās*. [Response: Regarding *karman*...
Because [the *kalā*] is exhausted merely by producing experience (*bhoga*), and because there is no other effect [to be produced], [it would be useless].

Furthermore, if action (*karman*) performed together with another principle (*tattva*) were not the cause of experience, then even the principles beginning with *buddhi* would be purposeless. [Objection: In that case, it was previously stated that the self’s knowledge and vision occur precisely through conjunction with *kalā*.

Knowledge arises through the conjunction of its constituent parts (*kalā-yoga*), while existing as a measure (*māna*) itself— just as the cognition of a jar arises from the contact of the sense organs with it.
And thus, the self (*ātman*) is indeed the substratum of knowledge.
If it is argued that [the self] does not possess the nature of knowledge, we say no; for the absence of ignorance in the self is due to its non-existence [as a property],
and furthermore, it is simply because of the absence of a manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*), just as there is no cognition of a jar enveloped in darkness.
This is because of the absence of manifestors such as lamps and the like, and not because of its non-existence; for if one were to admit that it possesses impermanent cognition,
it would follow that it too is impermanent due to its connection with modification,
[occurring] only when the manifestor is present.

Furthermore, because the nature of being a knower is established by one's own self-awareness, the conscious nature of the Self must be accepted as eternal; yet, due to being veiled by beginningless impurities, that [conscious nature] was not previously manifested before its connection with *kalā*, which serves as the manifesting agent.

Since [the soul] is designated as "limited" precisely through its connection with that [kalā], the connection with *kalā* must be accepted based on both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). It is precisely through this connection that the Self possesses limitation; enough of this elaboration.
And this is the connection with the three bonds (*pāśatraya*).

*Āvṛtaḥ*: He who is covered by beginningless impurity (*mala*) and by *karman* is called a *pralayākala*, because during the dissolution (*pralaya*), the *kalās* and other [categories] are withdrawn. *Vimuktaḥ*: He whose connection consists of only one bond, namely that called *pāśamala*, is called a *vijñānakala*. [This occurs] through the yoga of discernment (*vijñāna*) and renunciation (*sannyāsa*).
"And there is the exhaustion of karma through experience.

This is because, by means of *vijñāna*, there is also the absence of the bondage consisting of the kalās and so forth, which serve as the purpose for that [karmic] experience. Here, the terms *sakala*, *pralayākala*, and *vijñānakala* are used in the singular to denote the class (*jāti*). And they...

They are of two kinds: those whose impurities are fully matured and those whose impurities are not yet matured. Among them, those with fully matured impurities proceed toward liberation through initiation (dīkṣā) performed by a teacher who is of the nature of Śiva. As it has been said:

"Having joined these whose impurities are fully ripened to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) which causes their eradication, he [the teacher]— abiding in the form of the Preceptor (*ācārya*)— initiates them into the supreme reality; others, however, are transmigrating beings, including the *pralayākalas*, whose karma and impurities are either fully ripened or not yet ripened."
And there, one whose impurities and karma have been ripened attains liberation through initiation alone, without further ritual action.
As it is said in the Mṛgendra:
Upon the cessation of the authority of the power of darkness and its subsequent fall away,
Śiva reveals the infinity of vision and action inherent in the bound soul.
When this [world] of Svayambhū has perished, that [discipline] becomes twofold with respect to the supreme *niḥśreyasa* (final beatitude). Thus [it is said].

Others, however, being endowed with the body of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), are world-born embodied yogins; among these, some— by virtue of the grace of Ananteśvara according to the gradation of their maturation— attain the status of lords over the five groups of eight worlds known as Guhya, Atiguhya, Guhyātiguhyā, Pavitra, and Sthāṇu.
By virtue of her own authority, she becomes endowed with the powers of *aṇimā* and so forth, as well as manifest knowledge and action.
As it is stated in the *Tattvaprakāśa*:
"Having favored some, she bestows the status of a lord of the worlds... (6th line).

Their [powers] are such; and the portions of consciousness (*vijñānakalā*) are twofold, according to the distinction between immature and mature impurities (*apakvamála* and *pakvamála*). The mature-impurity portion belongs to the yogins who occupy the station of the Lord of Nescience (*avidyeśa*). The others, however, are the seventy million great mantras (*saptakoṭimahāmantra*). Even there, it serves as the means for the infinite realization of the goal and for the bestowal of grace by Śiva. For another purpose... (f9b, line 1)
"He is the instrument for the bestowal of grace upon the locus [of the soul].
This has been stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"In all [scriptural] paths, that [grace] depends upon the body of the one who employs it for that purpose."
Having brought about transformation at the end of its persistence, it enters Śiva, the Lord;
there is nothing else below the modification of Pradhāna except for the locus [of the soul].
Having performed its desired office, it attains dissolution during the withdrawal [of the universe]. Thus.
And thus, by the power of this mantra alone, the enjoyment of the worlds and liberation are attained by practitioners according to their desire. As it is said in the venerable *Sūkṣmasvāyambhuva*:
"Whoever should desire enjoyments in whatever [world], he is directed to that very [place]. (3rd line)
Thus, it is through the power of the mantras on the path of accomplishment and through the repeated practice of each respective [method].
And in the *Śrīmadraurava*:

"Those purified by initiation, born from the maṇḍala of the Guru Gaṇapati, are perfected beings (*siddhas*) whose bodies shine with the splendor of the orb of the rising sun; having experienced [the fruits]..."

"Having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time within the three classes [of beings], those whose ears have been pierced by this [teaching] become partakers of the sovereignty of the state of Supreme Śiva.
Now, it is said that for all [souls], the cessation of bondage arises through initiation (*dīkṣā*). How is this to be known? (5th line)
If it is argued that this is possible,
it is said in the venerable *Kālottara*:
"Having first performed the ritual of placing the jar as previously described, and having examined the heaviness of that self [of the disciple], one should proceed thereafter."

Having first performed its purification through the recitation of the *utpāda-mantra* and so forth, it is observed that lightness is produced in it again during the process of drawing [the arrow]. They say this is like the case of one bitten by a snake, where [lightness] occurs both before and after the treatment by the snake-charmer (*ahi-tuṇḍika*). And so it is stated in the *Tattvasaṅgraha*:
"Through initiation, one attains incomparable purity even from the primary sin of killing a Brahmin;
one should recognize the cessation of bondage through this sign, as in the case of the destruction of poison.
[Objection: But if all fetters (*pāśa*) are destroyed by initiation, does it not follow that the body would fall [die] at that very moment?
True. And initiation (*dīkṣā*) is of two kinds: that which brings liberation after death (*asadyonirvāṇā*) and that which brings liberation in this life (*sadyonirvāṇā*).
Among these, in the case of initiation that brings liberation after death, there is only the burning away of karmas that yield results in future births.
It remains established solely for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of prārabdha-karmas.
As it has been stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:

"The karma pertaining to various future states, like a seed with its atoms, is obstructed even while it is yet to come into being; for by means of that [karma], this [world] exists through experience. (3rd line)

However, in the case of immediate initiation into Nirvāṇa, that which pertains even to the *prārabdha* karma certainly occurs; nevertheless, it is possible only that the body remains for a short time. As it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*: (4th line)

Garuḍa: O Lord, if there is this severing of the bonds once initiation has occurred and the goal has been accomplished, how could there be a state of persistence? O Blessed One, it is just as when a jar has been produced and its completion has occurred.

"Even now, [he remains] because of the purification of previous latent impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), and likewise because this [body] was cast off by his own will; and he persists due to the force of latent impressions, having maintained his body through the power of *kṛt* and *bhṛta* [karmas].
Now, [one might ask: "In the case of immediate liberation through initiation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*), what happens to the karmas of a human being that yield results in future births? (6th [verse])

[Objection: If [the soul] remains for the sake of experiencing the *prārabdha* karmas, what is the fate of the karmas being performed during the bodily existence that follows initiation? For there is a rule that the fruit necessarily arises from a rite performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).
Regarding performance and the performance of prohibited acts—

meaning one should not, even in thought, transgress the conduct prescribed for one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramācāra*). Whoever, having received initiation whose essence is Śiva, should abide in whichever stage of life he occupies, he [should remain] in that very [stage].

"If one remains [in this state], one should protect the Śivadharmas. If it is argued that this is because of the scriptural statements such as "by transgressing the command, one becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years," and because of the hearing of the sin incurred by non-performance, it is replied:
The actions performed after the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) do not bring about results that pertain to another future birth;
rather, they persist according to the analogy of a burnt cloth.
As it has been stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya*: (2nd line)
"Even that which has been performed is like a seed sown in saline soil for the sake of attaining fruit.

Furthermore, after the initiation (*dīkṣā*), even those who have not practiced the conventional conduct (*samayācāra*) experience the state of being kings of *piśācas* for some time due to the fault of transgressing the command (*ājñā*).
Liberation occurs immediately thereafter.
And so it has been stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya*:
"Therefore, even though he had not performed the prescribed rites, the excellent king of the Piśācas, having become [a Piśāca] for a certain period of time..."

This pure-souled one attains equality with the Supreme through these [three]. And thus, regarding both the seed-initiation (*sabīja-dīkṣā*) and the seedless initiation (*nirbīja-dīkṣā*), there is not even a single thorn of doubt; so, enough of this digression. Thus [ends the discussion on] those to be initiated—the *vijñāna-kalas*.

Having described those divided by the distinctions of *praḷayākala* and *sakala*, [the author] now provides the seed of initiation (*dīkṣābīja*) in order to state that liberation occurs through the various types of initiation according to the gradations in the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*).
He speaks by means of the twofold nature of the first [category]: "The grace of Śiva is twofold: without support and with support.
The grace of Śiva toward the bound soul (paśu) is the desire for its purification and liberation; that is the seed of initiation (dīkṣā).
It is twofold through the distinction between being without support and having support. (Line 6)

That which proceeds without the support in the form of the Teacher is supportless (*nirādhāra*). But that which proceeds by presiding over the form of the Teacher is supported (*sādhāra*). Likewise, the All-pervasive One (*viśva*) is to be conceived as both supported and supportless;
thus it is both supported and unsupported (*sādhārā ca nirādhārā*). It is the totality (*sakala*).
"But as for that initiation of others which was declared to be without a support (nirādhārā),

he speaks of this very same [initiation] through a distinction of causes and also through a distinction of objects: 'The Teacher awaits Śiva [for this], because of the twofold descent of power (śakti-nipātana).'"

He himself bestows grace upon those who are *vijñāna-pralayākala*s. He is called *Śiva* because he "wills" (*vaṣṭi*) and "shines forth" (*prakāśate*); the meaning is that his nature is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*).

This is correct because the root *vaś* (meaning "to desire") is established through a transposition of syllables (*varṇavyatyaya*). This has also been stated by the wise: "Indeed, [he is] the destroyer... (*hiṃsi...*)
The word *dhātu* is [the root] *siṃha*;

in the sense of "subduing" (*vaśakāntau*), it is traditionally remembered as *śiva*. Thus, the transposition of letters is established. As for the term *paśyaka*, it is like *kaśyapa*: one who has disregarded the teacher, having entered into the very form of the Teacher, [perceives] the *vijñāna-pralayākala*s.

The *vijñānakalas* and the *pralayākalas* are divided into two types due to the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*). This twofold division arises from the distinction between "intense" (*tīvra*) and "more intense" (*tīvratara*) descents of power.
Among them, the descent of power is intense in the case of the *vijñānakalas*, while it is more intense in the case of the *pralayākalas*.
Therefore, even though the *pralayākalas* have attained the state of *vijñānakalas*,

the sense is that out of compassion— thinking, "They have been exhausted for so long in the offices imagined by me; now they shall be liberated"— He bestows grace (*anugraha*), which is known as the loosening of the bonds of *mala* and *māyā*.
He bestows favor.
As it has been stated by Cintyaviśva:
"By Śambhu, who is independent of [human] teachers and possesses intense power,
there is the formation of consciousness and the dissolution of the individual soul (asakala)."
"Whatever action is performed, that is proclaimed to be without a substratum.
Having thus described grace as being without a substratum, he speaks of that which has a substratum:
"By assuming the form of the Teacher, through the descent of the fourth power..."
The Blessed One bestows grace upon all of them as well.
The Blessed One is endowed with unlimited sovereignty and other qualities;
[namely] complete sovereignty, heroism, fame, and splendor.

And because of the scriptural statement: "The six—knowledge and dispassion, etc.—are called *bhaga*," [the Lord] bestows the fourth [type of] descent of power (*śaktipāta*) upon all beings, even those bound by the three fetters known as *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman*; this [descent] is of four kinds, termed *vrata*, *ripu*, *manda*, and *mandatara*.
By casting down his own power (*nija-śakti*), he bestows grace (*anugraha*)— that is, supreme grace (*aty-anugraha*). As it is said in the *Cintyaviśva*:

"Assuming the form of the Guru, Śambhu performs that initiation which possesses authority through devotion characterized by degrees such as mild, intense, and so forth"— thus it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*.
And Śambhu performs this [action] because of his autonomy and omnipresence;
being peaceful and bestowing grace upon all, he initiates [the disciple] by means of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).

Is it not the case that initiation (dīkṣā) is said to occur according to the varying intensity of the descent of power (śakti-nipāta)? For when power has been exhausted, the very occurrence of such a descent is impossible.
If it is argued that there is a gradation [in the descent], it is said in reply: the descent is metaphorically designated as being oriented toward the grace of power itself.
As it has been stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"In this world, the application of words is seen to occur through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*);
for example, the all-pervading Lord, though eternal and the knower, is said to be subject to destruction."
Just as the Lord Śiva, the king of mantras, was described regarding the severing of the noose,
so too has the descent of power (śaktinipāta) been taught for the devotee in the Śiva-āgama.
Just as the sudden falling of an object causes fear,
so too is the falling of a thunderbolt said to bestow the fear of worldly existence.
Just as a teacher awakens sleeping students with a staff before them,
so too does Śiva awaken those sleeping in the sleep of delusion by means of his power (śakti).
Alternatively, it is said that "it falls" refers to the knowledge of one's own true nature (*svarūpa-vijñāna*). Regarding its definition, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"I shall describe the definition of that fall according to the varying degrees [of capacity] among embodied beings."
Likewise, there is the falling of the body and trembling during the arousal of supreme bliss.

Sweating and trembling—this is the characteristic of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Thus, by means of the medium of the teacher’s form, Śiva alone is the initiator, because others lack the capacity to sever the entirety of the bonds (*pāśa*). This is so regarding that which is called the grace of Śiva.
He says that the activity [of initiation] arises there for those who desire initiation: "Initiation is born through the grace of Śiva for those who have performed their duties."

For those who have performed their duties and whose impurities have been ripened, initiation (*dīkṣā*) arises solely through the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*) by the grace of Śiva; the sense is that for others, there is simply no eligibility for it. Therefore, in the absence of the descent of power, for both the one to be initiated and the initiator—
Furthermore, a transgression is heard [in scripture],
as for instance in the case of Vāmadeva:
"Where power has not descended, there purity does not arise."
Neither knowledge, nor conduct at night, nor liberation, nor the supernatural powers (siddhis) exist [for one who lacks grace].
Therefore, having repeatedly observed the signs of the descent of power (śaktipāta),
the Guru should purify the disciple through either knowledge or ritual action.

"He who acts otherwise out of delusion perishes, being of evil intellect. Thus, having stated that the distinction between initiations (*dīkṣā*) arises solely from the specific excellence of the purification of the *idā* and other channels, he now promises to define the various types of initiation. And that [initiation]...

This manifold variety of the knowable is called its "proliferation" (*prapañca*). The sense is that this initiation (*dīkṣā*), which possesses a substratum (*sādhikaraṇā*), [is contrasted with] that which is without a substratum (*niradhikaraṇā*), because [the latter] is accessible solely through Śiva and so forth.
He now states those very modes, which are of many kinds, as they will be described in the subsequent explanatory passages.
There is the visual initiation (*cākṣuṣī*), as well as the tactile (*sparśadīkṣā*), the verbal (*vācikī*), the mental (*mānasī*), the scriptural (*śāstrī*), the yogic (*yogadīkṣā*),
the pertaining to the *hautra* office, and so forth, in many ways. Among these, that which is performed by means of the eye is the visual initiation.
The initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*) is accomplished by taking hold of the hand of Śiva; the verbal initiation (*vācaki*) is completed by the mere utterance of the mantra;
the mental initiation (*mānasi*) is to be performed through the activity of the mind; and the scriptural initiation (*śāstri*) is to be set in motion by the practice of the scriptures of Śiva.

Yoga-initiation (*yogadīkṣā*) is to be understood through the instruction on yoga (*yogopadeśa*). The sacrificial initiation (*hautrī*) is preceded by the preparation of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the mandala, the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), and so forth;

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is said that [the initiation] is indicated by the offering of water for the feet (*pādodaka*) and the stimulation of the senses. He states the definition according to the order of enumeration.

Having opened the eyes and meditated upon that reality, when the disciple is gazed upon for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the fetters, this is considered the ocular initiation (*cakṣuṣī dīkṣā*).
The meaning is that one should meditate on reality as having the nature of Śiva, while for others it is [meditation] by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

Therefore, meditation on the nature of Śiva is the seed of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Having opened his eyes for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the fetters—that is, for the release from the three fetters such as impurity (*mala*)—he gazes upon the disciple.
That which is perceived through the correct contemplation of identity with Śiva is expressed here by the present tense (*laṭ*) in the sense of a state of being (*bhāve*).
This initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed;

the use of the feminine gender is due to the proximity [to the preceding word]. It is a creeper belonging to the visual faculty (cākṣuṣī latā). Here, from the statement "having opened [the eyes], one gazes," it is understood that the eyes are closed at the time of meditation (dhyāna).
And so it has been said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Having closed the eyes and meditated upon the supreme reality (*paratattva*), one should then see [it] with pure vision;
for the sake of purification, this is considered the 'ocular initiation' (*cākṣuṣī dīkṣā*)."

In this context, the word "two-fold purpose" refers to enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). Now, regarding the initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*): having placed Śiva, conjoined with the Brahma-aṅgas, in his right hand, he should touch the disciple from the head downwards; this shall be the initiation by touch.
Here too, the phrase "having meditated on that" (*tattvaṃ dhyātvā*) is understood to carry over from the previous context, because the commencement of initiation (*dīkṣāpravṛtti*) is rooted therein.

[One should meditate on] Śiva, who is conjoined with the five Brahmans as his limbs (*brahmāṅga*) and endowed with the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*), [and on] the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) which establishes Śiva.

Because of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier, the preceptor— [the word] "his own" being understood as the remainder— having placed [the hand] on his right hand and having assigned [the mantras] to the fingers and the middle [of the palm],
should touch the head and other parts of the disciple.
One should touch the disciple from the head down to the feet; this shall be the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā).
Thus it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "Having meditated upon the supreme Śiva together with his limbs (the Brahmamantras) in his hand,
the Guru should touch the disciple’s body, beginning from the head and the back, down to the extremities."
"Thus, the initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*) occurs when it is performed by one who knows dissolution (*laya*) and enjoyment (*bhoga*).
Likewise, elsewhere it is said:
"Whomever he touches with his hand, whomever he beholds with his eye..."
"Everything becomes auspicious when struck by the rays of the moon of Śiva. Thus [it is said].

Now he speaks to the reciter (vācakin): "Having joined the two-fold [mantra] within the reality (tattva), with the splendor residing at the end of the *brahman*, one should utter the *saṃhitā* mantras; let this initiation of speech (vāgdīkṣā) proceed. Within the reality...
Having fixed the mind upon Paraśiva by means of unwavering concentration, and for that very reason,
[one becomes one] with the splendor of Śiva residing within the lotus pervaded by the supreme light that extends to the end of Brahmā.
The meaning is that the teacher (ācārya)—the subject understood from the context—is one whose state of identity with Śiva has been fully illuminated; this is for the sake of eternal [liberation].
The *saṃhitā-mantras* are the root [mantras] and the limbs of Brahman.
As it is said in the venerable *Liṅga-purāṇa*:

"This is called the 'Root-Brahma-limb' in the *Śaivasamhitā*. Thus one should recite it; indeed, one should recite it oneself for the purpose of purifying the disciple's sins. Let this initiation by speech proceed. The optative suffix (*loṭ*) is used here in the sense of possibility, meaning that the teacher should speak in accordance with [the disciple's] qualification.
As it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Having established the mind upon reality, which is illuminated by the splendor of the Lord, the Guru should utter the mantras; thus is the initiation by mantra (*mantradīkṣā*) accomplished."
"One should utter the mantras with speech; that is known as the *vācika* (verbal) initiation.
Thus [it is said]. Now he speaks of the mental (*mānasī*): "Resorting to the mental procedure, it is designated as 'mental' (*mānasī*)."

If all the rites, even while being performed externally starting with the purification of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa-mala*), are performed by the mind alone, then that is designated as *mānasī* (mental).
Likewise, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "Resorting to the mental rite, she [is] possessed of mental knowledge.
(4th line) Now, he speaks of the scriptural [initiation]: "By the transmission of the scripture, the initiation of the weapon (*śastradīkṣā*) is proclaimed."

By means of the instruction of the *Śiva-śāstra*, such as the *Kāmika* and other [Tantras]. This initiation into the *Śāstra* must be performed immediately after the consecration of the *samaya* vows; otherwise, there would be no qualification for hearing the *Śiva-śāstra*. For this very reason, the *Śiva-śāstra*...
Even hearing [the teaching] is indeed a specific form of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Thus it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"The initiation of the scripture (*śāstradīkṣā*) is declared to be the formal transmission of the scripture."
Now he speaks of the initiation through yoga (*yogadīkṣā*):
Through yoga, there shall be initiation through yoga; it is established in his state of Śiva-hood.
Through yoga—namely, through the practice of *dhāraṇā* and so forth, and through the instruction of yoga—there shall be initiation through yoga.
This has been explained by us at length in the *Dīkṣādarśa*; let it be understood there.

And this [initiation] is established and certain for the attainment of the state of Śiva for this disciple-soul; whereas for others, there is the attainment of the state of Rudra or the state of Īśvara.

The result arises from a disposition that conforms to one's specific qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, the meaning is that even this [practice] must be performed by one who has been consecrated through the initiatory rites (*samaya*) and so forth.
(From the *Cintyaviśva*)
In the sense of the verbal root *yuj* (to join), the union (*saṃśleṣa*) of both Jīva and Śiva is clearly called "Yoga," which is the path of the Self (*sahamārga*). Furthermore,
it consists of the destruction of the state of unreality and the manifestation of the state of true knowledge.
The union with the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is called the initiation of yoga (yogadīkṣā).
Then he speaks of the *hautrī* [line]: "The *rajaḥ-kuṇḍavatī*, that *hautrī*, is indeed said to be of two kinds.
Here, by the word *rajas*, the maṇḍalas to be accomplished through the colors corresponding to Īśāna and the others are meant.

[The initiations] are described as follows: having first prepared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the mandala, and having completed the external activities, the initiation consisting of the specific commitments (samaya-viśeṣa) and so forth is the *hautrī* [initiation]. And that is of two divisions, meaning it is of two kinds. [Objection: But surely, since this too is a single entity...

Since there is the possibility of many varieties, one might wonder how it is that there are only two types; anticipating this doubt, he says "in brief": "And this initiation (dīkṣā) is said here by those who know it to be twofold in its summary form. This initiation is the *hautrī* (pertaining to the *hotṛ*) for one who possesses the qualification (*sādhikārin*).
"By those who know that"— the ellipsis being "by the teachers (ācāryas) who know the true nature of initiation. Here, in this scripture, it is said that [initiation] is of two kinds,
of two types.
Regarding that twofold nature here: one is known as possessing knowledge, while the other is remembered as possessing action;
one is possessed of knowledge, and the other is remembered as being possessed of action.
In that regard, he states the characteristic of [initiation] for one possessing knowledge:
"Initiation for one possessing knowledge is said to arise from the correct awakening to reality, consisting merely of mental activity such as the rites of purification and fire."

Sacrifice (*ijyā*) is the act of offering; for it is stated that sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishing of a substance for the sake of a deity while the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is being performed, beginning with the oblations (*homa*). The "fire-rite" (*analakarma*) refers to the rites for the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the consecration of the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*), and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the pavilion, the mandala, worship, and the like are included—all of this [is performed] without [the aforementioned].

"Merely from mental activity" means that it has as its effect only the operation of the mind. And that initiation (*dīkṣā*), which arises from the thorough awakening to reality and is produced by the knowledge of the true nature of the collection of Śiva’s ritual acts, is called "possessing knowledge" (*jñānavatī*).
Otherwise, it would be incurable.
Thus it is said in the *Cintyaviśva*:

"The Guru, who is full and the bestower of the true path, should out of compassion initiate with the initiation of higher knowledge (*vijñānadīkṣā*) a disciple who has already been endowed with the previously mentioned initiation."
The initiation that occurs through the mere activity of the mind is revealed in due order;

that initiation is indeed the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*), which may also be called the initiation of higher realization (*vijñāna*). For therein Śiva-nature is bestowed and all doubt is destroyed.
Thus, because it possesses such a distinguished nature, it is designated as "consciousness."
Next, he states the definition of *kriyāvatī*:
"That [practice] which possesses sacrifice (*ijyā*) and fire (*anala*), and from which skill in action arises, is *kriyāvatī*.
Here, 'sacrifice' refers to the yoga consisting of the forest-dwelling mode of life (*vānaprastha*), and 'fire' refers to the sacrificial fire."
One who has been consecrated by the fire-rite possesses both [the fire and the ritual]; thus, in the case of one possessing the sacrificial fire,
[the result] arises through skill in action and the capacity for the teacher's rites, such as the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*).
The initiation (*dīkṣā*) that arises from skill in ritual action is "possessing action" (*kriyāvatī*). He states its division:
"Now, it is manifold, seedless (*nirbījā*), and with seed (*sabījakā*); [namely] seedless initiation and initiation with seed.
"Manifold" (*anekā*) means not being one; the meaning is that it is of two kinds. Now, the essential nature of both—(3rd)

In order to define the distinctions [of initiation], he first states the distinction of its objects: "Among these, that [initiation] is 'seedless' (nirbījikā) for the Samayin and the Putraka; however, it is 'with seed' (sabījā) for the Sādhaka and the Ācārya as well. Here, by the word "seed" (bīja),...
The practice of the *samaya* is now described. Devoid of that [practice] is the "seedless" (*nirbījā*);
indeed, the "seedless" is synonymous with "independent" (*nirapekṣā*). These are synonyms for the same meaning, applied to the initiate known as a *samayin*, and to the *putraka*.

It occurs when one is initiated as a "son" (putra). This teacher intends to make the initiate a "son" (samayin); the meaning is that this is what must be performed for him. And this [initiation] is of two kinds: the seedless (nirbījā), which leads either to immediate liberation or to liberation after death; thus he says. Now, that seedless initiation has been described.
It is of two kinds:
one is the immediate [liberation],
which bestows liberation immediately after initiation, granting *nirvāṇa* right then and there upon the falling away of the body.

This bestows liberation immediately after the fall of this body; it is a Nirvāṇa that occurs instantly. And because this [initiation] is for certain [people], he says: "For children, the ignorant, the elderly, women, those devoted to enjoyments, and those whose minds are distracted, there may be a seedless initiation (nirbījā-dīkṣā), devoid of the rules of conduct (samayācāra). Children are those who have merely undergone the thread-ceremony."

"Fools" (*bāliśāḥ*) refers to those who are ignorant; according to Amara, "fools" (*mūkhāḥ*), "blockheads" (*mūrkhavaidheyāḥ*), and "fools" (*bāliśāḥ*) are synonyms. "The elderly" (*vṛddhāḥ*) are those afflicted by old age. "Women" (*striyaḥ*) are those possessed of devotion (*bhaktimatyaḥ*). "Those who enjoy pleasures" (*bhogabhujah*) are those tormented by the desire for sense-objects (*viṣaya-abhilāṣa-pīḍitāḥ*). "Those whose bodies are diseased" (*vyādhitātmanah*) are those whose bodies are overwhelmed by diseases such as consumption (*kṣaya*) and leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). Of these—

The seedless initiation (*nirbījikā dīkṣā*). It bestows purity regarding the conduct of the rules (*samayācāra*). Since children and others lack the capacity to perform the observance of the rules of conduct, the rule of conduct is [fulfilled] at the very time of initiation.
In this [system], the teacher extracts and purifies [the mantras] according to the capacity and specific qualifications of various practitioners; therefore, it bestows purification.
Thus it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"For children, women, and others, without depending on the performance of pledges (*samaya*) and so forth... (3rd line).

And it is declared that the one called "seedless" (nirbījā) is independent of the granting of liberation. Because it does not depend on that [granting of liberation] for those who are incapable of observing the rules (samaya), such as the elderly, the dull-witted, children, the weak, and women, it is described as "independent. Now, the "with-seed" (sabījā) [initiation] is dependent [on the granting of liberation].
He states another synonym: "And for the wise and the capable, it is proclaimed as 'with seed' (sabījā).
For the wise—those possessing knowledge of the scriptures—and for the capable—those having the power to perform the conventional practices—it is "with seed.
This is another synonym for "dependent" (sāpekṣā).
That which has been proclaimed [is] what ought to be performed—this is the remainder [of the sentence].
And so it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:

"That which requires dependence upon the performance of pledges (*samaya*) and so forth, as well as upon the qualities of the self such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and other human virtues, is 'dependent' (*sāpekṣā*)."
And it has been declared that [the state] with seed is thus described. And it is said: "That which is the abode of Śarva, which follows the rules of conduct and so forth,"
"The wise say that *sāpekṣā* consists primarily of distinguished qualities of the self.

Now, he also states that *sabījā* is likewise twofold according to the distinction of its objects: "And *sabījā* is divided into two; the first pertains to one who possesses the nature of Śiva (*śivadharmiṇī*)."

That [initiation] for the practitioner and the teacher is said to be twofold, distinguished by the differences of place, time, and so forth, as well as by the distinction between initiation with seed (sabīja-dīkṣā) and [initiation without seed].

Among those, the first [is found] in the *Śivadharmottara*. And that has been taught according to the distinctions of place, time, and so forth for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*). The definition of place and time is given in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
Near a river, the ocean, a mountain, an excellent sacred ford, or a holy forest;
in a field of Śiva, a temple of Śiva, or an auspicious dwelling during a favorable planetary configuration.

"When the site has been purified and cleansed, one should construct a pavilion there. Thus, the characteristics of the initiation pavilion have been set forth by us and explained in detail in the *Dīkṣādarśa*; let that be understood from there. As for the time, it is precisely the time of the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*), according to its varying degrees; therefore—

It is precisely by virtue of the varying degrees of the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*) that the various types of initiation (*dīkṣā*), such as *sadyonirvāṇa* and others, come into existence. Alternatively, they may be understood according to the temporal divisions, such as the worldly time (*laukika*) and so forth, as taught by Trilocanaśiva and others. For example:
In the *Siddhāntaratnāvalī*:

"At the time [of the year] excluding the annual [festival], the month of Pauṣa, and Caitra; during a festival of the gods, at the giving [of gifts], at the solstice, at the equinox, or during an eclipse or the two solstices; [and] at the initiation or the Pavitra festival."

"In those created by Maitra, Arka, Anila, Saumya, and Pitṛ— namely Pūṣan, Śarva, Īśvara, Aja, and Rohiṇī— the triad of seasons [is established], excluding the day of the Earth (Mangala) and the Sun (Sunday).
Having thus stated the distinction of the subject matter in the *Śivadharma*, he describes its essential nature:
Action, consisting of both dharma and adharma, which has previously come forth in its manifold variety, is there contemplated and purified; that very state is declared in the *Āśivadharma*.

"Prāk" means previously accumulated. "Āgāmi" refers to that which is to be experienced in this life or in another birth, consisting of dharma—that is, having the nature of merit and demerit—and being manifold. Having mentally delineated all such karma, which is diverse due to the variety of its experiences, [the practitioner] purifies it therein, in that [state].
By the power of such gifts, that very [soul] is rendered capable of producing fruit according to various enjoyments; this is declared to be the initiation into the Śivadharma.
(2nd line) *loka*...
He states the nature of *dharmanī* (the cosmic order): "In the purification of mere *adharma*, the second [form] is in the *lokadharmanī*.

Having established the karma of mere *dharma* for the sake of the true enjoyment (*sadbhoga*) in those respective worlds and so forth, [it exists] in the purification of mere *adharma*—that is, the purification of all *adharmas*. (Third line)

When purification has been performed in the manner described, there is the word *sāmasetyamātra*. This is the second [initiation], known as *lokadharmiṇī*. It is the initiation with seed (*sabījadīkṣā*).
For this very reason, it concerns the dharmas for the sake of enjoyment in those various worlds (*bhuvana*) that are required within the worlds.

"In this" means "in that which possesses worldly attributes (*lokadharmiṇi*). "Possessing the attribute of Śiva" (*śivadharmiṇi*) means "Śiva-nature belongs to this. Furthermore, the meaningfulness of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is twofold, distinguished as higher (*parā*) and lower (*aparā*). Among these, the higher is the direct cause for attaining the state of Supreme Śiva (*paraśivatva*).

But another [type of yoga], distinct from the dissolution of the body, is the cause for attaining the state of Supreme Śiva after experiencing desired enjoyments as one pleases in worlds of enjoyment, by means of a divine body assumed according to one's own will.
Thus it is stated in the *Bālajñānaratnāvalī*: (6th line)
