"The root of the Śiva-dharma is the body, and its fruit is the glory of the Śiva-dharma; there is no destruction [of this] until the dissolution of the body on earth," thus it is said regarding the worldly dharma (*lokadharman*), which is twofold through the distinction between the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). Among these, the higher is as follows: in each respective world (*bhuvana*)... [two folios are missing].

The former is the cause for attaining the state of Śiva only after the body has passed away for one who has already experienced worldly enjoyment. The latter, however, bestows the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* even upon one who seeks enjoyment, immediately after the body has fallen away.
As it has been stated in the *Bālajñānaratnāvalī*:
"When the portion of [karmic] evil has been destroyed in all the planes of enjoyment,
the remaining [portion] is desired by the disciples for the sake of the body and the powers such as *aṇimā*, according to the worldly dharma."

The supernatural powers (*siddhis*), such as *aṇimā* and so forth, are both "with stain" (*sāñjana*) and "stainless" (*nirañjana*). Among these, those "with stain" are established through the yoga systems of Patañjali and others; those "stainless," however, are established through the efficacy of the practice of Śaiva mantras.
As it is stated in the Kāmika:
"The attainments resulting from desire are to be known as [the lowest]; the attainments of the Brahmic state are remembered as [the highest];
kingship is the inferior [attainment], and the attainments of the caves are the middling."
The supreme state of being a *khecara* and the equality with the most excellent deity exist in many ways, each distinguished by categories such as the status of a *vidyeśvara*.
These include the status of a *vidyeśvara*, the state of a *rudra*, the state of a *brahman*, and the station of *vaiṣṇava*.
Whatever happiness exists in the abodes of Rudra, such as Māyā, Kārya, and Īśa, is [transient].
"But another [result] is the state of abiding in the station of Ananta and other [deities] through supreme knowledge.
Thus concludes the determination of eligibility for initiation (*dīkṣā*) according to the previously mentioned Śivadharma and Lokadharma systems.
He now defines its essential nature (*svarūpa*) by another method; as it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "It is as follows:"

Initiation for the sake of liberation is of two kinds: that which follows worldly dharma and that which follows the dharma of Śiva. That which follows worldly dharma is to be known as belonging to householders, while that which follows the dharma of Śiva belongs to those who bear the sectarian marks (*liṅgin*). Where there is no cutting of the topknot (*śikhā*), that initiation follows worldly dharma.

That initiation which is joined with the cutting of the top-knot (*śikhā*) belongs to the subject characterized by Śiva. Likewise, in the purification of the *māyā*-principle, one should completely burn away the top-knot in that [initiation].

"Because it is reckoned as having Śiva as its inherent nature, that initiation is for one who possesses the nature of Śiva (śivadharmī). That initiation which is without the cutting of the top-knot (śikhā) and so forth is for one who possesses worldly nature (lokadharmī).
Likewise, in another case as well, by means of initiation, [one becomes] of worldly nature."
"The Guru should initiate a householder who follows the Śiva-dharma; likewise, he should initiate those whose wealth is austerity (tapasvins) who follow the Śiva-dharma.
Furthermore, he states that there is a twofold division of authority based on the distinction between having authority and lacking authority, due to the difference in their respective domains.
Because the entitlement [to rites] pertains only to the permanent [initiation], the occasional initiation— even for one who is a *samayin* or a *putraka*—
is indeed devoid of entitlement. Regarding the occasional initiation,
it does not grant entitlement to rituals such as consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth, even for those who are *samayins* or *putrakas* who are unfit for such entitlement.

Because the qualification for [the rites] belongs exclusively to those who are permanent [initiates], initiation is for those without qualifications; that is, it is devoid of qualifications such as those for occasional rites (*naimittika*) and so forth. He states that for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*), it is with qualifications.

Because the practitioner and the preceptor possess authority in all matters— whether in obligatory, occasional, or optional rites— that [authority] belongs to them. (5th line) Precisely because these two, the practitioner and the preceptor, possess authority over all rites among the obligatory, occasional, and optional ones, that [authority] belongs to them.
The initiation of those two, the practitioner and the preceptor, is indeed authoritative.
In the Kālottara [Tantra] (6th line):
"The triad beginning with the daily rite (nitya) must be performed by the teacher during exposition;
the daily and the optional (kāmya) rites for the practitioner are as stated in his own scripture, O Six-faced One."
"It is proclaimed that [this] always applies to both the *samayin* and the *putraka*.

Thus, now, showing that the distinction in characteristics for the *samayin*, the *putraka*, and the *sādhaka-ācārya* arises precisely from the difference in their initiation (*dīkṣā*), he says: "Where there is yoga in the state of Rudra..."
In the state of the Lord of Yoga and Vidyā, where there is no cutting of the topknot (śikhā-cheda), that initiation is of two kinds, pertaining to the Samayin.

In that [initiation], the one in which the disciple is joined to the station of Rudra during the initiation of the pledge (samayadīkṣā) is the first; that in which the disciple is joined through yoga to the station of Īśvara is the other.

That [initiation] is the *samaya-dīkṣā*. It is of two kinds where there is no cutting of the top-knot (*śikhā-cheda*). This is merely a description of its essential nature, because in the case of the *samaya-dīkṣā*, the absence of the cutting of the top-knot is established as a matter of fact; it is not included within the formal definition (*lakṣaṇa*), since the cutting of the top-knot is already precluded by virtue of being an ancillary part of the *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*. And so it is said:
The definition is stated as follows: one who has been consecrated by the *samayadīkṣā* that leads to the state of Rudra is a *samayin*;
one who has been consecrated by the *viśiṣṭasamayadīkṣā* that leads to the state of Īśvara is a *putraka*.

Thus, it is stated that by the mere initiation of the *samaya* (vow), one attains the state of Rudra; and by the two specific types of *samaya*, one attains the state of Īśvara. Now, he explains that for the *putraka* (spiritual son), there is the initiation of *nirvāṇa* (liberation) which is devoid of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Wherein there is the severing of the bonds and the crest-lock, there occurs the union in the state of Śiva.
That very initiation which is called *nirvāṇa* is for the *putraka*;

it is that in which the cutting of the bonds (*pāśa*) and the topknot (*śikhā*) occurs during initiation. It is the cutting of the remaining thread and topknot at the locations of the five *kalās*, beginning with *nivṛtti*. And wherein there is union with the deity Śiva, that initiation for the *putraka* is indeed called *nirvāṇa*.
The meaning is that he should be one who has performed the rite; that is to say, he must be one who has received consecration (*abhiṣeka*), not one devoid of consecration.
And thus, the meaning is that even a son who has been initiated into *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā* [is qualified], for even in the case of *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*...
By the initiation with the mantra to be accomplished, one is a practitioner (sādhaka); by the initiation with all the vidyās, one is a master (ācārya)—so he said.

She is proclaimed for the practitioner during the consecration of the mantra to be accomplished; through the consecration of all vidyās, he enters the domain of the Ācārya. For whomsoever there may be liberation by means of a mantra, there is no dependence on the accomplishment of the *aṇimā* siddhis.
And that mantra becomes effective for him immediately.

By means of that mantra, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is proclaimed as the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the practitioner (*sādhaka*); likewise, the defining characteristic is that the practitioner is one consecrated by the mantra to be accomplished (*sādhya-mantra*). However, through the consecration of all the sciences (*sarva-vidyā*), [he is empowered] by all mantras.
But that initiation by means of consecration (abhiṣeka) occurs within the domain of the teacher— that is, in relation to the teacher—
and thus the definition is stated: "one who has been consecrated in all the vidyās is an Ācārya."

Having thus understood the six thousand-fold body, one should diligently perform the dissolution (*laya*) and enjoyment (*bhoga*). If a teacher performs initiation without knowing dissolution and enjoyment, he shall be cooked in the Raurava hell along with his disciples. Therefore, the instructor should perform the initiation only after having understood it through diligent effort.

One should practice thus. Having thus established the different types of initiation (*dīkṣā*) according to the distinction of qualification for the sake of knowledge of the seed of initiation, [the author] concludes the section on the scriptures (*nigama*).

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is considered to be of every kind: it is the conferral of the state of Śiva upon one who has been joined with the purificatory rite of Śiva, whether by means of ritual action (*kriyā*), or by the power of constraint (*bādhaśakti*). It may be performed through ritual action preceded by the construction of a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), or else by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-dīkṣā*), which consists of mental activity.

Or rather: for one who is joined with the *śiva-saṃskāra*— that is, for one who has received the purification (*saṃskāra*) performed by Śiva, whether with or without a substratum (*sādhikaraṇa* or *niradhikaraṇa*)—
because the bestowal of the state of Śiva (*śivatva-samarpaṇa*) occurs, therefore that [purification] is divided into many types, such as the previously mentioned visual and so forth.

Initiation (dīkṣā) is considered to be threefold among all bound souls (paśus), being divided by the distinctions of *pralayākala*, *vijñānākala*, and *sakala*. The meaning is that it should be performed according to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and in accordance with their respective qualifications (*adhikāra*).
Likewise, in the Vāmadeva [Upaniṣad]:
"By means of knowledge... the teacher of conduct should purify the disciple."
Having thus established the initiation (*dīkṣā*), he concludes by way of its bestowing the fruit:
"By initiation, the embodied one (*dehin*) is liberated from the threefold bond of existence.
The word *dehin* is used in the singular to denote the entire class [of beings]. Even the threefold animal (*paśu*) [is liberated] from the threefold [bond].

One is liberated—that is, one becomes free—from the bonds of existence, from the snares of saṃsāra consisting of impurity, māyā, and karma. Now, in order to describe the thorough knowledge of the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhiparijñāna*) as well, since it serves as the seed for initiation (*dīkṣā*), he says that the path is sixfold: "And that initiation is the complete purification of the paths; and that path is traditionally taught to be sixfold."

That initiation which liberates one from saṃsāra is the purification of the paths (*adhvasaṃśuddhi*). That initiation, consisting of the purification of the paths, has the path as its constituent limb; and the path is traditionally said to be sixfold. He indicates these very [paths] according to the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*): the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*), the path of words (*padādhvan*), and the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*).
The path of the worlds, the path of the principles,
and the path of the creative powers enter into the single state of Śiva.

Alternatively, even that which is sixfold in form—consisting of mantra, word, phoneme, world, principle (*tattva*), and aspect (*kalā*)—merges into the one, supreme, and primary Śiva, known as the station of the *śivatattva*; it enters therein through initiation (*dīkṣā*), this being the implied meaning. And thus, when the purification of the six paths beginning with mantra has been performed by means of initiation, they are condensed into the *śivatattva*.
Just as for seeds burnt by fire, there is no further capacity for experience;

thus it is understood that for those liberated through Śiva (śaivamuktāḥ), liberation consists in the manifestation of the Śiva-principle (śivatattva) through union with it—this principle being the supreme of all—by means of initiation (dīkṣā). Regarding the creation of the liberated, the Lord says: "The difference between the [liberated] person and the [created] person..."
By virtue of this statement, because there is no returning again from below the level of Śivatattva, being devoid of re-entrance is indeed the state of supreme liberation.
[Mantra, etc. (f18b1st line)

Having contemplated that purification must be performed by means of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), each being more pervasively encompassing than the one preceding it, he explains that very manner of pervasion: "Mantras are pervaded by words (pada), and those [words] by phonemes (varṇa); therefore, everything is [pervaded]. Phonemes, in turn, are pervaded by worlds (bhuvana), and those [worlds] by... (2nd line).

Having thus contemplated those principles (tattvas) as pervaded by the kalās, one should purify them here in sequence; likewise, the five paths are to be purified. Mantras are pervaded by words (padas), and words by phonemes (varṇas);
phonemes by worlds (bhuvanas), worlds by principles (tattvas), and principles by kalās.
Having thus contemplated that even the five *kalās* are pervaded [by these principles] and contain within them the five paths (*pañcādhvan*) in succession, they are to be purified.
And so it has been stated by Trilocanaśivācārya:
In this context, the mantras are pervaded by the words, the words by the syllables,
those syllables by the worlds, and those worlds likewise by the *tattvas*. This pervasive activity is known as the impurity of delusion (*mala*).
Those [elements] which are pervasive with respect to existence also enter into the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader; these are the *kalās* grasped here by them.
This indeed is the state of the *kalās* as the five paths (*pañcādhvagabhūtatva*).

In order to establish this very point, he also states their common purificatory correspondences: Cessation (nivṛtti), Stability (pratiṣṭhā), Knowledge (vidyā), and Peace (śānti) reside in the sky [of consciousness], extending in sequence from the heart, throat, palate, and brow to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). (6th line)

Here, by the word *nābhasī*, the *śāntyatītā* is meant. Because of its connection with that [state], one should contemplate these kalās— namely *anivṛtti*, *pratiṣṭhā*, *vidyā*, *śānti*, and *śāntyatītā*— in their respective order within these locations, from the heart up to the throat, the palate, the eyebrows, and the *brahmarandhra*.

The syntactical connection is "they are to be purified. Now, for the purpose of purifying the five paths beginning with *tattva* within the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, he describes the method of summary in sequence: "In Nivṛtti, the single earthly *tattva* is to be meditated upon."

The syllable *kṣam*, the city of Kalā, Agni, and the others numbering one hundred and eight; from the final word down to the word *mahādeva* in reverse order; the twenty-eight words beginning with *vyomavyāpin*;
and Sadyojāta and Hṛdaya—these two [constitute the sequence].
The two mantras have been proclaimed.

From the qualities (guṇas) and smell (gandha) up to sound (śabda), the five Brahmans are the cause. In the Nivṛtti-kalā, the earth-tattva—the single earth-element—is present; having included the object of meditation and purification, it is to be internalized within the path of the tattvas.
The syllable, however, is the letter *kṣa*. On the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), there are one hundred and eight worlds (*bhuvana*) consisting of the cities beginning with Kālāgni.
This is the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), which proceeds in reverse order from the final word up to the word of Mahādeva.

Counting the words of the *vyomavyāpin* mantra in reverse order, there are twenty-eight. This is the path of words (*padādhvan*). The two heart-mantras beginning with *sadyojāta* constitute the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*). [The path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) consists of] smell and so forth, ending with sound: the qualities (*guṇa*) of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. Brahmā...

And there is another reason: [5th line] Now, it will be stated immediately thereafter that in the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the twenty-four principles (*tattva*) beginning with water (*ambu*) are to be purified.

Therefore, why is a summary of those beginning with smell (*gandha*) and ending with sound (*śabda*) stated here in the context of cessation (*nivṛtti*)? In that regard, [the summary is given] because of the [correspondence] of smell and the others with the principles (*tattva*).
Summary:

(6th line) Here, there is no contradiction in [regarding them] as qualities (*guṇa*). Now, one might object: "In this context, it is not appropriate to include the qualities such as fragrance (*gandha*), etc., because they lack the status of being 'paths' (*adhvan*); [only] the purification of the paths (*adhva-śuddhi*) is intended."
If it is argued that this is indeed initiation (*dīkṣā*), that is true;
for when purifying the principle of earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*), since its related qualities must also be purified, let it be so.

Nevertheless, because fragrance and the other qualities are themselves to be purified, they do not exist [as the principle itself]. How then [could there be purification] for the Lord who is the cause?

If it is asked what the summary of "the state of being purified" is, here [it is said]: for the sake of bestowing grace upon the king who has gone to the state of Śiva, the summary of Brahman consists precisely in the removal of bondage by making it favorable;
indeed, this is for the purpose of purification because he possesses authority over the earth-tattva. Now, the manner of summary within the *pratiṣṭhā*-kalā:
He said:
In the Foundation (pratiṣṭhā), the principles beginning with the limbs and ending with Nature— numbering twenty-four— are to be known by their essential nature.
The twenty-three phonemes from *ṭa* to *ha* in reverse order,
as well as the fifty-six cities beginning with Amareśa, are to be known.
There are twenty-one words beginning with Maheśvara and ending with Arūpa;
there are two mantras, Śiras and Vāma, and four are remembered as the Guṇas.

Viṣṇu is the limit of the words beginning with *rasa* and ending with *śabda*, and the reason for this is explained by the recitation itself. Now, he states the method of summary regarding the *vidyā-kalā*. (4th line)
In the Vidyā-tattva, the seven principles beginning with Puruṣa are to be known in their proper sequence;
likewise, the twenty-seven worlds beginning with Vāma are to be understood.
Starting from the word "Vyāpinī," they extend up to "Dhyānahara."
There are twenty words; the two mantras Śikhā and Ghora are established [therein].
From the letter *ka* to the letter *gha*, there are seven syllables in reverse order.
Form, touch, and sound are the qualities (*guṇa*), while Rudra is the cause.
This also is explained by the words themselves. Now, he states the method of abbreviation regarding the *śāntikalā* (the sixth line).
In the Śānti [kalā], however, there are three principles: Vidyeśvara, Sadāśiva, and the three phonemes Ga, Kha, and Ka; the two mantras that pierce the faces and the body;
and Vāmā as the primary among the eighteen principal puras by enumeration.
The eleven words beginning with *nityayogina* and ending with *vyomavyāpina* have been stated here in reverse order. Therein,
the pair [of letters] *sparśa* and *śabda* is the twenty-second cause.
This too is explained by the words themselves. Now, he describes the method of summary regarding the *śāntyatīta-kalā*:
"But in the *śāntyatīta-kalā*, the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) is established."
In this [system], there are fifteen puras, beginning with Nivṛtti;
the single word-mantra "Oṃ" is for the Astra, and it consists of the three beginningless Śivas.
The sixteen phonemes, starting from the Visarga and ending with the letter 'A', are proclaimed [here].

"Sound possesses a single quality, but Sadāśiva is its cause. This too is explained by the very words used (nigadavyākhyāna). Since an explanation is possible for these [qualities] precisely according to the order of their enumeration and the sequence in which they will be discussed, it is thus [stated]. (3rd line)

Having explained the method for the condensation of the paths (*adhvan*), he states that [this] should also be meditated upon within the principles of Śakti and Śiva: "Thus, having contemplated the paths, one should then meditate on the Supreme Pervasive One (*vyāpinī*) through the six paths; above those Śaktis, one should meditate on the Supreme State. (4th line)
Having contemplated the path— including all six paths— in the manner of the previously mentioned summary (where the singular is used for the class),
one should then meditate upon the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), who pervades the six paths and is the very essence of that pervasion; above her is the Supreme Power.

One should contemplate the supreme state above, which is synonymous with *laya* and known as the *śivatattva* state, because it is therein that the liberated ones abide; this is for the purpose of uniting the disciple—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. [This applies] to all the *tattvas* situated below the *śivatattva*. (6th line)

The etymological meaning is that the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) is indeed difficult to conceive within the state of [ordinary] mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*); furthermore, such cultivation must be preceded by perfect knowledge, for it cannot be conceived through ignorance. Therefore, this alone is the supreme seed of all initiations (*dīkṣā*).
Thus, [this is] the summary of the Madhva... [f20b, first line].

Having stated this, [the author] pledges to explain that since it is impossible to understand the nature of the *adhvan* without knowing its summary, those very *adhvans* and their divisions which are useful for initiation (*dīkṣā*) are these [that will be discussed]. Now, regarding those useful for initiation... (2nd line)
The division of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is described here in detail according to their sequence. "In detail" (*vibhāgaśaḥ*) means being spoken by way of division.
He states the division of the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*): Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Ghoratattva, Puruṣa, and Īśāna, as well as Hṛdaya and Śiras. (3rd [verse])
At the base of the crest-armor weapon (*śikhavarmāstra*), the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*) is proclaimed.
These are the mantras of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna, as well as the mantras of the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapon.
Together with the root mantra, all twelve mantras have been proclaimed.
As for the sequence of their extraction, it is as follows in the *Kāraṇa*:
It is produced by the collection of the sixteen vowels, excluding the neuter ones,
and is endowed with the syllable called *nāda* through the collection of the twelve vowels.
The letters corresponding to ether, fire, and earth, as well as the seventh and the ninth [vowels],
joined with the bindu and nāda, are called the five Brahmans.
The twice-born [should worship] Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna,
ending each with a salutation (namaḥ), following the sequence of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa):
namely, with the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth [mantras].
The six limbs are prescribed by means of [mantras] consisting of ten and twelve syllables.
The heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the eye,
and the weapon— these are proclaimed as the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in their proper sequence.
From the heart up to the eye, they are declared to be joined with the nasal bindu (m).
The weapon, extending as far as its discharge, is endowed with the six classes [of beings].
In the sequence of *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *hum phaṭ*,
these indeed constitute the "five-fold birth" (*pañcajāti*) when joined with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and the others up to the end of the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Having placed the *praṇava* at the beginning, one should immediately follow it with the utterance of *kha* (or *ka*).
The utterance of the limbs of Brahmā, preceded by a salutation and ending in the dative case,
is honored in all ritual activities;
likewise, it is described in the *Kriyākaraṇamaṇḍana*.
In the group of non-effeminate vowels (a, i, u), there are nine, six, and one [syllables] respectively;
one should utter the short seed-syllables of Īśa, Pumān, Ghoratara, Vāma, and Aja.
In that same group, there are five, four, three, and two [syllables] for the meditations on the lines.
These syllables are proclaimed in sequence as the seed-syllables for the heart and other limbs:
the sixth [consonant] ending with *s* (sa), joined with *ja* (ja), *bha*, *ri*, and endowed with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and the sound (*nāda*).
This mantra, [known as] Saṃpradānaśiva, is to be applied to the heart, the heart, and the navel. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*, the extraction of the root mantra is as follows:
"One should join the sixth seed-syllable to the fifth seed-syllable following the heart-seed;
one should place a bindu upon the head, conjoined with three morae."
"One should know that such a Śiva exists in all castes in due order.

And regarding the distinction of application (*viniyoga*), it is stated in that very same place: "One should arrange the ends of the short, long, and protracted [vowels] according to one's desire or at will."
In this context, the term *hrasva* (short) refers to the Brahmans; the term *dīrgha* (long) refers to the ancillary mantras (*aṅga*); the term *pata* refers to the root mantra (*mūlamantra*);
and the term *ananta* refers to that very [mantra] up to the level of *samanā*. Thus it has been explained by Aghoraśivācārya. (6th)
A short [mantra] burns away sins; a long one certainly effects eradication.
One should employ the *pata* for nourishment and in the rite of infinite liberation. Thus it is said.
It is also stated in the Viniyogapaṭala:
"In that very [text], one should employ mantras joined with 'namas' at the end for worship;
for fire-offerings (homa), those joined with 'svāhā' at the end are used for rites of pacification, attraction, and nourishment."

"And they should be employed in rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), joined with the utterance of *svāhā* at the end. Now, one might object: "Since there is a statement in the *Bambāgama* that 'the Brahmans [mantras] are to be conceived as short, while the limbs (*aṅga*) are long,' the Brahmans must be pronounced only in their short forms. And so it is said:

According to the rule that the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) do not possess short vowels (*hrasva*), how can it be said that the *okāra* and *ekāra* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa? For it has also been established that the *ekāra* and *okāra* possess shortness (*hrasvatva*) within the skin (*tvac*).

As the authors of the Śikṣās have said: "Among the auxiliary sciences of the Veda (chandaḥ-aṅga), the Sāmatas, Ugrīs, and Āraniyas recite the short *e*-vowel and the short *o*-vowel. [Objection: But how can it be that only the root-mantras are the limbs of the Brahman, given the phrase "the path of the mantras" (*mantrādhvā*)?

It is said: because it is impossible to purify the seven crores of great mantras during initiation, since all of them are included within these very [mantras] and because it is precisely these that are employed as the objects to be purified. (4th line)
Since it has been stated that [this] is the nature of the path of mantras (mantrādhvatva), there is no contradiction.

Having thus described the paths of mantras, he now states the essential nature of the path of words (padādhva): "In this way, the path of words is proclaimed to consist of exactly eighty-one words. Regarding these eighty-one words and their phonemes (varṇas)...
The determination [of the mantras] by way of their upward progression is precisely that; and they are set forth in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as follows:

"Om"—this single syllable is there the first word, whose nature is Śiva. The second is indeed the five-syllabled word "vyomavyāpine."* *(Note: The asterisked line corresponds to the 6th line of the source text.)*
The third step, for the one whose form is space, should consist of five syllables.
The fourth [syllable] shall be five-colored; it is the all-pervading word.
The three-syllabled word is "śivāya," and these are the words for the five limbs.
For Ananta, it is "anantāya."
The four-syllable word for the designator is "vācakam";
the four-syllable word for the subtle is "anāthāya";
and the five-syllable word for the unsupported is "anāśritāya"—this was spoken by Śiva as the non-designator.
The three-syllable mantra *dhruvāya* is the designator of Ekanetra;
the four-syllable mantra *śāśvatāya* is the designator of Ekarudra.
The eight-syllable mantra [is for] Trimūrti, who is established upon the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*).
The five-syllabled word is the eternal abode of Śrīkaṇṭha for the yogin;
the five-syllabled mantra is the designator of Śikhaṇḍin for one whose sustenance is meditation.
The six-syllabled word "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya" is that of Gāyatrī.
The five-syllabled mantra of Sāvitrī is the word for universal manifestation;
the three-syllabled "Śivāya" is for the worship of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas).
The six-syllabled mantra of Īśāna is "Īśānamūrdhe."
The seven-syllable mantra for Puruṣa is "puruṣavaktāya";
for Bahurūpin, it is "aghorahṛdayāya," also consisting of seven syllables; and for Vāmadeva, the seven-syllable mantra is "vāmadevaguhyāya. (4th line)
The seven-syllable mantra for Sadyojāta is "sadyojātamūrtaye.
Then there is "oṃ namo namaḥ," which consists of five syllables and denotes Caṇḍa.
The five-syllable phrase "jyotirūpāya" is its [Sadyojāta's] word, and it denotes the Astra-mantra.
Then follows the heart-mantra of six syllables, beginning with the word *guhyāt guhyatara*.
The two-syllable word *goptre* is considered the designator of the head (*śiras*).
The four-syllable mantra is for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the word *nidhanāya* is considered [the mantra] for this [armor].
The armor (*kavaca*) consists of seven syllables beginning with *sarvavidyādhipāya*.
The word for the weapon (*astra*), consisting of five syllables, begins with *jyotirūpāya*.
The eye (*netra*) is said to have eight spokes and begins with *parameśvara*.
Furthermore, the six limbs of Caṇḍanātha have been declared;
his seat consists of seven syllables beginning with "acetanācetaneti. The term "vyomavyoma" is to be known as the four-syllabled mantra of Dharma.
The pervasive, all-pervading, four-colored syllable is the designator of knowledge.
The formless, formless [syllable] consists of six syllables for detachment.
"First, first"—this consists of six syllables for sovereignty.
The word *tejas* with four syllables is the term for the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
The word *jyotis* with four syllables is considered the term for its center (*anta*). It is held that there are thirty-two syllables for the filaments (*kesara*), both below and above.
"Arūpa-anagni-adhūma-iti, then the word abhasma;
likewise, anāde, adhanā, nā, nā, dhū, dhū, and dhū— these seven words,
each consisting of three syllables, are found in the Śiva Āgama."
Oṃ *bhūḥ* is the two-syllabled mantra; *oṃ bhuvaḥ* consists of three syllables.
*Oṃ svaḥ* has two syllables, and *nidhanam* has four syllables.
*Nidhana* should be known as three syllables, while *nidhanodbhava* consists of five syllables.

The word "Śiva" is considered a two-syllable term, and "Sarvapa" is also considered a two-syllable term. The Supreme Self (*paramātman*) consists of four syllables, and Maheśvara likewise consists of four syllables. Mahādeva consists of four syllables and expresses the Lord of True Being (*sat-bhāveśvara*).
The four-syllable word *mahāteja* is the station for the Lord of Yoga;
the five-syllable word *muñca muñca* is considered a four-syllable station (*padam*).
The six-syllable word *prathama-prathamā* is likewise proclaimed as a station.
Śarva-śarva-catur-varṇa, likewise Bhava-bhava,
and Bhavodbhava-catur-varṇa— [these names] bestow happiness upon all beings.

The eight-syllable [mantra] is for the purpose of bringing all things into proximity; the seven-syllable [mantra] is likewise. "Worshiping Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Supreme One," and "the unworshipped, the unworshipped"—these are the four phrases consisting of eight syllables each, as established previously in the Śiva Āgama.
(7th line) There should also be thirty-two filaments, according to the tradition;
the word *sākṣin* (witness), repeated twice, followed by the four castes (*caturvarṇa*), shall be the expression for the petals.
The eight stations of Indra and the others will be described in sequence as follows:
*caturvarṇa*, *turuturu* (six times), *pataṅga pataṅga*, *vai*,
*piṅga piṅga* (four syllables), and likewise *jñāna jñana* is considered [the eighth].

The word *śabda* consists of four syllables; likewise, the word *sūkṣma-sūkṣma* consists of six syllables. The two-syllable word *śiva* is considered the all-pervading word among the eight bearers of the directions.
The three-syllable word is considered the all-pervading word among the lords of all vidyās.
Oṃ namo namaḥ is considered the five-syllabled word, the head of Brahman.
Oṃ śivāya is the four-syllabled word denoting Rudrāṇī. Namonamaḥ is considered the four-syllabled word in the Pāśupata system.
The single syllable "Oṃ" is to be meditated upon as the designator of the Vajra and the other [deities].
It is taught that there are three hundred and sixty-eight phonemes (varṇas), and eighty-one words (padas); thus is the path of words (padādhvan) proclaimed. So it is said.

And likewise, in the *Kālottara* in six thousand [verses], after explaining the words in the chapter on the Description of Śiva’s Body (*śivatanu-varṇana-paṭala*), the restatement of that [text] and the number of syllables are set forth at the very beginning of the chapter on the True Nature of Śiva (*śivasadbhāva-paṭala*). As follows: "Now, the number of Śiva is declared..."
(5th line) Three hundred and sixty-eight syllables have emerged from Śambhu’s secret mantra; and the half-mantras were previously proclaimed by Vidyeśāna— thus it comes to pass.
Now he speaks of the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*):
"The path of phonemes is proclaimed as that which begins with the letter *a* and ends with the letter *kṣa*. This is indeed a self-explanatory statement.

Now, by means of describing the inclusion [of all things] within the principles (*tatva*) of the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), he states the summary regarding the *kalās* as well, through the very delimitation of their respective efforts.
The worlds of Kālāgnirudra, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Hāṭaka, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Rudra— these six are situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
The skull-bearer, the one whose banner is raised, the Buddha, the diamond-bodied, the crusher;
the pervasive lord, the imperishable teacher, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the sovereign of the thirty gods;
the fire, Rudra, the consumer of oblations, the tawny-hued, the devourer, Hara.
Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, Kṣayāntaka;
Yājya, Mṛtyu, Hara, Dhātṛ, and likewise Vidhātṛ, the Supreme;
Kartṛ, Vaktṛ, Viyoktṛ, Dharma, and likewise Dharmapati.
Nirṛti, Māraṇa, Hantṛ, Krūradṛṣṭi, Bhayānaka,
Ūrdhvaretas, Virūpākṣa, Dhūmra, Lohitadamṣṭrin, Bala, Atibala, Pāśahasta, and Mahābala.
Then Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghahasta, Jalāntaka, Meghanāda, Sunāda—the tenth—is proclaimed;
[and] Śīghra, Laghu, Vāyuvega, Sūkṣma, Tīkṣṇa, and Kṣayāntaka. (5th line)

The ender of the five, the one with five locks of hair, the one with matted locks, the one whose vehicle is the clouds; the lord of treasures, the beautiful one, the fortunate one, the one of gentle form, the wearer of matted locks; the bearer of prosperity, the bearer of the earth, the glorious one, the bearer of life-force, and the one who bestows grace at will.
In the [direction] of Vidyādhipa and Aśani: Sarvajña, Jñānadhṛk, Vedapāraga; Sureśa, Śarva, Jeṣṭha, Bhūtapāla, Balipriya;
Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Ranta, Krodhana, Māritāśvana.
Grasara, Dṛmañjarīśa, Phaṇīndra, Vajradaṃṣṭrin, Śambhu, Dhabhurgaṇādhyakṣa, Trayakṣa, Tridaśeśvara,
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, Nabha, Līpsa, and Trilocana.
Vīrabhadra and Bhadrakālī; above all [these] are two worlds.
Since these verses are merely indicative in nature, the establishment of their meaning is easily accomplished through a simple word-by-word analysis.
Now, regarding those [worlds] mentioned at the outset, it was stated that the six Brahmās are in the middle of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). (Third line)

Others, however, maintain that there are ten Brahmāṇḍas in each direction starting from the east, as well as two worlds for each path; he establishes their division by including the word "etcetera" (ādi).
Kapālīśa and the others are in the east; Agnirudra and the others are in the southeast; those beginning with Yāmya are in the southern quarter; those beginning with Nirṛti are in the southwest;
those beginning with Bāla are in the western quarter; and those beginning with Śīghra are in the domain of Vāyu (the northwest).
In the north are Nidhīśa and the others; in the northeast are Vidyādhipa and the others;
in the lower region are Vṛṣa and the others; and above them are Śambhu and the principal deities.
They are established in the ten directions outside the Brahmāṇḍa.
Now, in this way, he summarizes that the hundred and eight worlds, beginning with Kālāgni, are withdrawn into the *nivṛtti-kalā*. Thus,
by enumerating the ancient cities beginning with Kālāgni, [their dissolution] should be understood as occurring within the *nivṛtti* and subsequent *kalās*.

One hundred and eight. Having thus described the worlds situated within the principle of Nivṛtti, he now describes the worlds residing in the principle of Pratiṣṭhā, beginning with the element of water.
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiśa, Puṣkara-auṣadhi,
Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍa, Bhārabhūti,
Lakuḷīśvara, Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Jalpeśa, Āmrādikeśvara, and Madhyameśa.
Mahākāla, Kedāra, Bhairava, as well as Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nākhalo, and Nakhala; Vimaleśa, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and Bhīmakeśvara;
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Vimukta, and Mahābala.
Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu; Chigalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, and Maṇḍaleśvara; Kālāñjaya, Śaṅkukarṇa, Stūleśvara, and Sthaleśvara. (4th line)
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, and Aindra;
likewise, the Saumya should be known, as well as the Brājheśa and the Brāhma as the eighth.
Also the Akṛta and Kṛta, the Bhairava, and the Brāhmavaiṣṇava.
The Kaumāra, the Cauma, the Śrīkaṇṭha, and likewise the eighth.

Thus, he makes a division of fifty-six by means of the number eight times eight, [distributing] the established portions of the principles (tattva) whose names have been thus indicated among those seven principles.
Amareśa and the others reside in the principle of Āptatva; Hari, Īśvara, Indra, and the rest in Tejas; Gayā and the others in Vāyu; Vastrāpada and the others in Vyoman;
Chagalaṇḍa and the others in Ahaṃkāra; and the Paiśāca and other [groups] are situated in Aham.
Including Prakṛta and Kṛtādya, there are thus fifty-six cities.

These [eight] should be known within the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā] by the names Amareśa and so forth. Therein, Amareśa and the others are proclaimed by the names of the Ādiguhya-aṣṭaka, Atiguhyāṣṭaka, Guhyātiguhyāṣṭaka,
Pavitrāṣṭaka, and Sthāṇvaṣṭaka, by the command of the Supreme Lord for the sake of favoring the worlds.
And he becomes one who dwells in the world of beings and is of the nature of the *liṅga*.
Thus it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The eight Rudras of the primary secret (*ādiguhyāṣṭaka*) and likewise the eight of the supreme secret (*atiguhyāṣṭaka*)."
The eight secrets of the secret, and also the eight purifiers.
And Sthāṇvākāra—these five, by divine appointment, dwell upon the earth;
established as *liṅgas* for the sake of favoring the worlds.
O Six-faced One, that which is situated near them is Toṣa.
That sacred ford is supremely meritorious; having bathed there, one shall go to Śiva.
Those men who always give up their lives at these stations pierce through the cosmic egg and go to the state of the five-fold eightfold [Brahman].

And this [type of] supreme liberation, which consists of the reality of liberation produced by bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), residing in the abodes of Śiva (*śivakṣetra*), and so forth, is [merely] a preliminary; the supreme liberation, however, occurs through initiation (*dīkṣā*) alone.
It has already been established that apart from that, there is no supreme liberation whatsoever.
Then Vidyākalāvatī spoke of the worlds: Vāma, Bhima, Ugra, Bhava, Īśāna, Ekavīraka,
Pracaṇḍa, Umāpati, Aja, Ananta, and Ekaśiva.
Krodha, Caṇḍa, Dyutīśa, Saṃvarta, Lakuṭīśvara,
Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, Śikhoda of great splendor,
Vāmadeva, Udbhava, Bhava, and Ekapuṅgala.
Ekeṣaṇa, Īśāna, and likewise Aṅguṣṭhamātraka—
now he effects their division according to the distinction of the principles (*tattva*):
in the *puruṣa*-principle of Vāmā and the others, there is the pentad beginning with Pracaṇḍā, located in *rāga*.
In [the worlds of] Niyati and the others, in [the worlds of] Krodha and the others, in [the worlds of] Mahādyuti and the others, and in the illusory [worlds],
there are twenty-seven cities of Vāmā and the other goddesses, as well as those of the Vidyās. Now, they describe the worlds of the Śāntikalā.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālikalavikāriṇī,
Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathanī,
Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī— these are the infinite [powers].
Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Rudra, Trimūrtika, Śrīkaṇṭha, Śrīśikhaṇḍin, and likewise another, Sadāśiva.

In Śānti, there are eighteen worlds belonging to the left face. Here, within the worlds of the Śāntikalā, in the principle of Vidyā, there is [the series] ending with Manonmanī, excluding the creator of the mind (Manonītikāra). In the principle of Īśvara, there is the group of eight beginning with Ananta; in the principle of Sadāśiva, there is Sadāśiva.
Thus.
Now he speaks of the worlds beyond Śānti;
as for the nature of Nivṛtti and the others, it is stated in the Mṛgendra-tantra: "Those powers by which [the Lord] effects the unfolding of human splendor..."
These are the lords of the worlds designated as Vṛtti and the others.

Just as the cessation of crops occurs when the time for their growth has passed, so too do the beings belonging to those realms cease; that place is called Nivṛtti, and its lord is likewise named Nivṛtti.
For one who has desisted from worldly activity, the movement that repeatedly manifests as a characteristic of the past is restrained;
that is the *pratiṣṭhā* (the state of stability), and he who possesses it attains its lords.
Through this, [the Lord] bestows upon the individual soul (*aṇu*) the knowledge whose object is the realm accessible to the self through the principles (*tattva*).
That is his field of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), and he is the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*),
for by that [knowledge] Hara brings about the pacification of all his sufferings;
it is peace (*śānti*) and that very state (*pada*), and by effecting that, he too becomes possessed of peace (*śāntimān*).
Those [energies] beginning with Indhikā, by which the worlds of objects above and below are made great, greater,
and greatest, through which one is liberated from consciousness—
those indeed are the stations throughout the three nights.

Even though [the soul] possesses omniscience and other qualities, it does not possess the state of being "joined" [to the body] due to a portion of impurity (*mala*). That by which its state of being a knower is established is its liberator; that is the state [of liberation], and he who performs the action of liberating it is the Lord (*īśāna*) who brings about that [state].

He is *Urdhvaga*, and his Lord is *Urdhvagāpati*. Those who have attained that state through the yoga of Śiva-sādhā also reach that supreme state after experiencing the bliss that lasts until the end of their stay there.
"And they do not perform creation and so forth, because they are established in their own self-interest, O Arhat.
Thus he concludes the enumeration of the worlds:
"In this way, there are two hundred worlds existing within the five kalās."

That which was described as the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) consisting of two hundred and twenty-four [worlds] is easily understood here; by the statement that "two hundred and twenty-four worlds have been described," it is implied that other worlds mentioned in various divine scriptures (*divyāgama*) are also included within this very [path] during initiation (*dīkṣā*).

By this much purification alone, their purification also becomes possible. Thus, having [discussed] the path of the worlds (*abhuvanādhvan*), he speaks of the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*). Now, the thirty-six principles are: earth, water, fire, air, and space;
Smell, taste, form, touch, sound, the organ of generation, and the anus;
the feet, the hands, the nose, the tongue, the eyes, the skin, and the ear;
the mind, the ego, and the intellect; as well as primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*).
Passion (rāga), necessity (niyati), knowledge (vidyā), limited agency (kalā), time (kāla), and the deluding power (mohinī);
then knowledge (vidyā), the Lord (īśvara), the Indescribable (sādākhya), power (śakti), and Śiva—thus they are traditionally remembered.
This is the explanation of the words as they stand. Of these principles (tattvas), beginning with earth... [3rd line].

The essential nature [of this] has been described in detail in the *Mṛgendra*, the *Matanga*, the *Sarvajñānottara*, and other Āgamas, as well as in the *Tattvasaṅgrahanirṇaya*, the *Tattvaprakāśa*, and so forth; therefore, it is not described here for fear of excessive length.
Now, he explains the path of *kalā* (*kalādhvan*).
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise the other, Atītā—these are the five kalās; this is the explanation according to the literal text.

Now he concludes this seed of initiation (*dīkṣābīja*) which has been established by means of the text: (5th line) "The enumeration of the six paths. Thus, the remainder is that the enumeration of the six paths—consisting of mantras and so forth—has been performed for the purpose of fully understanding the seed of initiation. [Thus, by the venerable resident of Vyāghrapura...]
In the *Vilocana* commentary on the *Varuṇapaddhati* composed by Nigamajñānadeva, the first section, the *Dīkṣāprakaraṇa*, [is concluded]. Homage to the illustrious Tripurasundarī!
The virtuous ought to forgive the offense committed by me.
(7th line) Salutations to the venerable Gurus, accompanied by Śrī Bālāmbā and with the assistance of the Lord of Vedapura.
[The Section on Consecration] (f27a,
1st line):
Now, having thus established the seed of initiation (*dīkṣā*), in order to establish each individual seed in accordance with the sequence of the enumeration, [the author proceeds].

He states the definition of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*): "Consecration is the offering of knowledge into the self-natured *liṅga*, the bestowing of the power of action, and the union with the pedestal according to the prescribed rule; and that [consecration] is fivefold."
The power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) alone is the very nature of the Self. Within that *liṅga*, there is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

The ritual offering (*samarpaṇa*)—the "perfect offering" (*sam-arp-aṇa*)—of the pedestal (*piṭha*), which is the nature of the power of action, into the base (*piṇḍikā*) according to the prescribed method, namely by way of the ritual form taught in the Śiva scriptures, is itself the yoga, the connection.

The meaning of the sentence is that this is called "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*). And this is the general definition. Here, by the word "dedication" (*samarpaṇa*) [in the fourth line], there is a joining together with a teacher who knows the established tenets of the Śiva doctrine and possesses skill in the thorough knowledge of the nature of gnosis and action.
That which is intended to be expressed [is as follows]:
if its true nature is not fully understood, even the act of connecting with it is difficult to accomplish.
By this, it is stated that the Master’s very capacity for knowledge is the primary seed of his authority (*pratiṣṭhā*). Likewise...

And the very union of Śiva’s power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is the ultimate referent of cognition. In reality, too, the power of knowledge— which is singular and has everything as its object— is itself the manifestation of multiplicity within that which is not non-existent.
The statement "it goes" establishes Śiva’s status as the agent of all things;
in that state, it is called the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and since the independent one is the agent, this pertains to agency.

Because it contains autonomy within itself, the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is metaphorically designated as that which establishes autonomy; thus, the power of will is also included within the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) alone. And so, because Śiva possesses a formal manifestation (*mūrtatva*), [the powers are present].

It is metaphorically designated as "the embodiment of knowledge" (*jñāna-mūrti*). And this "embodiment," being like an embodiment, is indeed partless (*niṣkala*). For this very reason, its nature as an "embodiment" consists in being the essence of both the *liṅga* and the *pīṭha*.
Thus it makes known [the truth], and likewise [the scripture] declares: "The pervasive [Śiva] is the embodied limb of Śiva, dissolved within. It thus manifests [this].

Thus [ends the first line], and [it refers to] the linga and the image. That which manifests it—the consecration performed by a preceptor skilled in knowledge and action—is what occurs immediately thereafter. By this very fact, the internal nature of Śiva’s power of knowledge [is established].

And it is indicated that the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is internal. That very [power], whose characteristic has been explained, is "Pratiṣṭhā" and is fivefold, consisting of five modes. He now enumerates those very modes.
Pratiṣṭhā, sthāpana, sthitasthāpana, and utthāpana are proclaimed;
therefore, it is also called sthāpana. This is a self-explanatory statement.
He states the definition of the arrangement of the objects for these [deities] according to the order of their enumeration:

"The Bāṇas and others should be joined, respectively, to the *piṇḍaka* preceded by the installation of the Brahma-stone in the *liṅga*, or separately on a pedestal (*pīṭha*) in a ruined or manifest [shrine]."

Regarding the placement of the *brahmaśilā*: in whatever direction or with respect to whichever *liṅga* the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is being performed, that [direction] is said to be the "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhe*). The pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) should be joined; the meaning is "the pedestal alone. (6th line)

The rite of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) performed upon that [image] such as an arrow and so forth is called "installation" (*sthāpana*). When there is no separate pedestal (*pīṭha*), the rite of consecration performed upon that [image] made of metal, wood, and so forth is called "establishment of what is already situated" (*sthitasthāpana*). When [the image] has become worn out...

In the case of a *liṅga*, the procedure for the renovation of an old one (*jīrṇoddhāra*) is what is meant by "raising" (*utthāpana*). In the case of a manifest form such as an image (*pratimā*), the procedure performed is called "installing" (*sthāpana*).
This has been stated by Trilocana Śivācārya:

The pedestal (pīṭha) is Umā and the liṅga is Śiva; the union of these two is declared to be *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration), as prescribed by the rules. That [consecration], whose body consists of the powers of will, knowledge, and action, is said to be fivefold: in the liṅga beginning with the Brahma-stone when it is joined with Śiva, and in the pedestal during the rites of *sthitapratiṣṭhā* (the consecration of what is already installed).

"Only the installation of the arrow (*bāṇasthāpana*) [is performed] for the image (*bera*) and the silver [liṅga], while the installation of the *arthātthāpana* [is performed] for the others. Having thus established the fivefold nature of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), he again states another definition of consecration according to a different opinion.

That installation which is endowed with the arrangement of the forms and the lords of the forms, along with the principles (*tattva*) and the lords of the principles, is eightfold and fivefold according to the rule. The principles are known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva;
the lords of the principles are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara. Just as it is accompanied by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), so too is the arrangement of the forms and the lords of the forms eightfold.

Or [the rite may be] fivefold. In that regard, there are eight forms (*mūrti*), beginning with Earth and ending with the Sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Within these forms, [the deities] range from Śarva to Bhīma. There are five forms which are the five elements, whose guardians are the Mūrtipas; furthermore, the Lords (*īśvara*) are formed by the group of five beginning with Brahmā. The ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is that in which the placement (*nyāsa*) of these [deities] occurs.
Regarding the phrase "the foundation of karma" (line 6), the ellipsis is to be supplied as "it is stated in a certain alternative view.
Their essential nature and the distinction between their objects will be clarified later by the author himself in the root text. Now, [the discussion continues].

Since the thorough knowledge of the removal of the [defining] marks (*lakṣaṇoddhāra*) is also the seed for the foundation, he states certain distinctions: "When the portion of Rudra is divided into three according to the Brahma-line, one should hang the *lakṣma* (mark) down in the two lower parts as far as the water-receptacle. When the portion of Rudra—the part for worship—is divided into three by means of the three parts... [and so on].

The meaning is that it has been prepared according to the central meridian in the middle portion. In the two lower parts— that is, in the two lower sections— the characteristic is that which rests upon water, [namely] water itself.
One should hang it down as far as the upper part of the pedestal; one should suspend it.
As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"The Guru, having divided the high [measure] of the Rudra-portion into three parts, should discard the uppermost portion.
Here, a specific rule regarding the "blazing" (*dīpta*) is also mentioned in the *Kriyākāraṇa*.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the Brahma-sūtra and its linga.
Having fashioned the linga as devoid of [external] form, one should place it within the portion for worship.
One should divide the entire portion for worship into sixteen parts.
"In the tenth [square], one should again draw the extraction of the eyes with a golden needle.
Here, it should be understood that the "tenth-ness" begins from the top.
Next, he states the width and length of the lines for the characteristic being extracted.

In the left part of the *liṅga*, at the twenty-fourth division, there is the loss of *lakṣaṇas* due to the Lord (*Īśa*). From that point, at the ninth division, the earth becomes low and the lines are lost due to forgetfulness.
(5th line) Regarding the length of the *liṅga*, at the twenty-fourth division—having calculated twenty-four divisions of the Buddha-part—the Buddha-parts are twenty-four.

This is the established tradition. The meaning is: "having made the length of the *liṅga* one part. (6th line) "The width of the *lakṣma*" means the extent of the mark; it should be made with one part—this is the ellipsis. The earth-line (*pṛthvī-rekhā*) and the location of the base for the lines are [determined] by the width of that line.

The meaning is as follows: having divided into nine parts that single portion which has been accepted as the measure for the width of the *lakṣma* (the central mark)— out of the nine hundred units that constitute the width between the two animal-lines—
one should act so that the width and the depth of the interval between the lines are each equal to one of those parts.
Next, he states the definition of the wing-lines:
"From the middle of the mark, two wing-lines [are drawn] in that field divided into eight parts."
Due to the rotation of six and seven parts at the back, that junction which arises from the visarjana—

starting from the half-lakṣaṇa (lakṣmārdhāt)— the two wing-lines (pakṣarekhe), meaning the two side-lines (dvipārśvarekhe), are to be drawn. In that field, within the area of the two side-lines, it is divided into eight parts.
Having divided that space into eight parts and excluding two below— having set aside two parts below, or six parts,
or seven parts— one should draw a circle like a half-moon using a cord half the length of the field's measurement.
The meaning is that one should rotate [the instrument] until the two lines meet upon the back of the *liṅga*.
That alone is common [to all].

Having explained the rotation for the [drawing of] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), he states the specific procedure for one who desires the continuity of prosperity (*bhūtisantāna*): "In that field divided by fire, by rotating two and a half parts, for the sake of the continuity of prosperity of the characteristics, excluding the lower half. (5th line) The meaning is: "In that field"—that is, in the field consisting of the two lines previously mentioned—"divided by fire" means having made it into three parts.
In that case, by excluding the lower half; having excluded the lower half, because of the rotation of two and a half parts,
that rotation which occurs in two parts is the half [of the whole].

From that rotation in the manner previously described, this mark (*lakṣma*) serves for the sake of the prosperity of the lineage (*lakṣaṇasantati*), meaning it leads to the continuity of the lineage and to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*); this is the implied sense. And likewise, in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Possessing the quality of half a *laṃba*" (7th line).

Having performed [this], one should rotate it for the sake of whichever portion [is intended]. That half-measure, according to the sūtra, is for those who desire prosperity (*bhoga*), liberation (*mokṣa*), or both. Thus, these two aforementioned methods are common to both prosperity and liberation;
however, regarding the distinction of results such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), [the procedure differs].

He says that it must be done otherwise: "Otherwise" means in a different manner; and the establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*)—whether through the distinction or non-distinction of the function of bestowing commonality—is established by the authoritative scriptures (*śāstra*) themselves. This should be observed in each respective instance. [The second part of the *Pratiṣṭhābīja*...]
This definition of the brother-in-law (jamātṛ), as well as this extraction of the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇoddhāra*), is fourfold according to the distinction of objects;
as stated in the *Dīptatantra*:
The *gavākṣa*, the *mahiṣākṣa*, and the *khaḍgāgra* in the form of a hollowed palm;
the *gavākṣa* is said for the Brāhmaṇa, while the *khaḍgāgra* is for the Kṣatriya;
the *mahiṣākṣa* is for the Vaiśyas, and the *karapuṭāgraka* for the Śūdra.
The method of collective arrangement in the form of hollowed palms for all [the fingers] is thus set forth in the *Kāmika* as the ninefold extraction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇoddhāra*). As follows:

The tip of the *liṅga* may resemble a bud, or the eye of an elephant, or it may have five facets; it may be shaped like a plantain bud, or like the point of a trident, or like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree;
or it may take the form of the tips of the weapons of the world-protectors, or the tip of Śiva’s own weapon.
"O twice-born one, the characteristics of the *liṅga* of all regions are now being told.

This definition as well should be seen as stated in that very same [text]. Here, by the word "characteristics," even the seed of installation (*pratiṣṭhābīja*) residing at the head [of the *liṅga*] is [intended], for fear of excessive prolixity in the text.
The author did not state this; and it is as found in the *Suprabheda*:
"The teacher (*ācārya*), together with the *śilpins* and the *lakṣaṇas*."
One should fashion the head, which is said to be of four kinds:
the first is umbrella-shaped, the second has the form of three peaks,
the third is like a hen’s egg, and the fourth is half-moon shaped.
Having made the neck (*tāra*) one-sixth of the height of the *liṅga*, and likewise the head (*śiras*),
one should then divide the remaining portion into nine parts; the middle part, extending as far as the depth,
is declared to be of variegated form (*cchitrākāra*), which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Having made the *tāra* (the diameter) six parts, it is rounded with a height of two and a half parts;
thus it shall have the form of three *puruṣas*, bestowing the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
In that very place, however, there is a *akuṇḍa* (a secondary pit) rounded with half the width [of the main pit].
Having divided the *liṅga* into three parts and excluding two of those parts,
this half-moon (*ardhacandra*) is described there in sequence;
thus is it stated in general.

Having stated the definition of the *lakṣoddhāra*, he demonstrates the systematic arrangement: "The opening of the eyes is the characteristic in the manifest; both manifest and unmanifest in the [objects] that are manifest-unmanifest; and in the *liṅga*s consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest, the characteristic is said to be the unmanifest alone. In the manifest [objects] such as images, it is simply the opening of the eyes; [and] in the manifest-unmanifest... (third line).
The remaining sense is that the characteristic mark should be made on the facial emblems (*mukhaliṅga*).

Now, he states that certain things should be avoided regarding the aforementioned characteristic mark: "In those [emblems], when there is instability at the beginning of the nine [lines] and so forth, even in the case of one made of copper or a gem..."
"The extraction of the characteristic marks (lakṣaṇoddhāraṇa) must be performed"—this is the completion of the sentence.
Likewise, in the Kāmika [Tantra]:
"This is not intended for a liṅga made of jewels, nor for one of iron, nor for one of lead."
Neither in the Bāṇaliṅga nor in the Raudra, nor in those originating from rivers or springs, is the natural form the defining characteristic; rather, it is the radiant luster found in gems.
In gems born of water or earth, the presence or absence of auspicious marks (lakṣma) may or may not be determinative.

Having thus shown the characteristics of the *liṅga*, he now shows the characteristics of the pedestal (*pīṭha*). In the middle of the cavity (*randhra*), the shape of the vulva (*bhagākāra*) at the tip of the thighs is the mark of the pedestal (*lakṣmapīṭhaka*). By one-third of that very cavity, at its base, one should fashion a bee-hive (*bhramara*). That which resides on the pedestal, situated upon the pedestal, marked by the marks of the marks—within the middle of the cavity, its form is that of the vulva, and it is fierce (*ugra*).

Furthermore, at the base of that [pedestal], by means of exactly one-third of the opening (*randhra*), there is a circular base (*bhagākāra*); at its base, that which is joined with a revolving line (*vibhrama-rekhā*) in the form of a bee (*bhramara*) is the pedestal (*pīṭha*)—
this is the immediate connection.
The meaning is as follows: having divided the cavity of the pedestal into three parts like the *liṅga*, and leaving the upper part aside,
one should rotate [the tool] like an *aśvattha* leaf so that the base of the vulva-shaped [pedestal] is formed by the two lower parts,
according to the lines characterizing the *liṅga*.
It should be made with the same width and depth as before, endowed with the aforementioned lines, because it consists of *śakti*.
As it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"The characteristic of its upper part is that which enters the aperture (*randhra*) and has the shape of a vulva (*bhaga*)."
"By which that supreme secret, consisting of power, is not seen by worldly people"—thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*. And [it says]:
"In the center of the aperture, having the form of a vulva with its tip pointing upwards, situated upon the seat of the *lakṣma*."
"In this manner, the wise preceptor should draw the marks with a golden stylus.

Having thus described the process of marking the linga and the pedestal, [the author] explains that after the series of ritual acts prescribed by the author of the *Pratiṣṭhāpaddhati*— beginning with the sprinkling of honey and ghee— the following must be performed regarding the Lord Tatveśvara.

He describes the specific bases for the installations of Mūrti, Mūrtīśvara, and so forth, according to their distinctions: "I [shall describe] the pervasion of the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the stone (*śilā*) in sequence, starting from the principles (*tattva*) and so on, up to Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, and Īśāna; one should again conceive of them as three sections. This is the pervasion of the *liṅga*, the pedestal, and the stone.

The remainder [of the sentence] is that [the pervasion] of each pedestal by means of the *liṅga* occurs through the sequence of pervasion (*vyāpti-krama*), not by means of the stone. Immediately thereafter, in those [pedestals],
starting from the *tattva*s— that is, according to the sequence of the emanation of the *tattva*s— there is the pervasion of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara, just as in the case of the *liṅga*.

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the state of Śiva [is as follows]: one should conceive of the principle of Power (*śaktitattva*) in the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the principle of Sadāśiva in the stone (*śilā*), and furthermore, one should conceive of the three-fold division (*trikhaṇḍa*) [of these]. (6th line) One should conceive of the pervasion of the three-fold division for each of the linga, the pedestal, and the stone.
He explains that very process: "From Vidyā, Śakti, and up to Śiva; Māyā possesses the power of space (deśa-śaktika);

[this continues] up to Śabda, Citta, and Sadāśiva—at the Liṅga and the Pīṭha, according to the sequence of the cremation grounds. The meaning is this: at the bottom is the Liṅga consisting of Śuddhavidyā, and in the middle is that which consists of Śakti.
At the end, one should meditate upon the three sections as being of the nature of Śiva itself, in the manner of the pervaded and the pervader, within the liṅga alone.

Likewise, on the pedestal (*pīṭha*) as well, there is the nature of *māyā* at the bottom, the form of Sadāśiva in the middle, and the essence of the principle of Śakti at the end; thus is the pervasion of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍavyāpti*) upon the fire-stone (*agniśilā*) at the base.

One should contemplate the pervasion of the three sections as follows: the first consists of the elements beginning with earth and ending with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); the middle consists of the organs of action and so forth, ending with the intellect (*buddhi*); and the final section consists of that which begins with the *guṇa-tattva* and ends with Sadāśiva.
Thus, one should meditate upon this threefold pervasion.
Likewise, in the Kāmika [Tantra],
one should again conceive of the three sections ending with Śiva-śakti-manīṣā;
then that which ends with Vidyā-śakti-Śiva, and [the section] consisting of Māyā-śakti.

The sequence [of the paths] from the word, the mind, and the end of the location, up to the sign and the stone, follows in order. Now, as an incidental discussion regarding the consecration of a temple (*prāsādapratiṣṭhā*), [the text describes] the pervasion of the paths (*adhvavyāpti*) therein by means of the heart, the jar, and the seed-syllable of consecration, along with the conceptualization of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍakalpanā*).

He also said: "The pervasion of Māyā-tattva and Antaka is proclaimed as being within the Heart-vessel (hṛtkuṃbha). Furthermore, the path of the three sections (trikhaṇḍādhvan) extends from the mind (citta) up to the end of Kalā and Māyā. Within the Heart-vessel, which constitutes the limbs of Prasāda and Pratiṣṭhā, Māyā resides at the root, the middle, and the tips."

The remainder [of the verse] is that there is pervasion up to the end of reality (*tattva*) by means of meditation. Now, he describes the pervasion of the paths (*adhvan*) and the conceptualization of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*) of the *prāsāda* mantra—which is to be invoked as the embodied form within the heart-vessel (*hṛtkuṃbha*)—by way of its being the embodiment of the person (*puruṣa*). "The lineage of the person consists of three sections, extending up to the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*). (6th [verse])
The threefold division of the Person (puruṣa), designated as the Palace (prāsāda), consists of the conceptualization of three sections,

extending up to the limit of the Word-Person (śabdapuruṣa). In sequence, at the base, middle, and top, it extends to the end of the principle of Sound (śabdatattva) and the end of the principle of Intellect (buddhitattva).

And here, the mention of the *puruṣatattva* within the temple is for the purpose of making known the state of the *pralayākala*. Thus it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Having invoked the *ātmatattva*, one should place it within the vessel like a jar."
[He perceives] the pervasive Lord, who abides as the inner nature of all beings, whose essence consists in favoring [souls] through their karma,
and who is endowed with the impurity of office (*adhikāra-mala*), along with *niyati* and the other *kalās*, as well as *māyā*, *rāga*, and *vidyā*.
"Having meditated thus upon [the self] as being stuck in the throes of birth, one should restrain it"—so they declare.

Furthermore, the nature of the Person in the Palace (*prāsādapuruṣatva*) is due to its specific character within the form of Śiva; this is to be understood in detail from the commentaries on the *Mataṅga*, *Svāyaṃbhuva*, and other scriptures.

The method of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in the heart-vessel (*hṛtkumbha*) is as described in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "The Guru should install an object shaped like a vessel (*kumbha*), elevated like a golden star or similar [metal], and filled with gold, jewels, and so forth, in the manner of a *liṅga*.
Alternatively, he may install a golden male figure (*puruṣa*) one *tāla* in height, or even one the size of a thumb, endowed with all the characteristic forms."

Having performed the bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances as before, one should place [the deity] upon the *kulikā* between the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the altar (*vedi*). Having meditated upon the Person (*puruṣa*), who is the embodiment of the jar (*ghaṭa*) and is free from dissolution (*pralayākala*), one should install him there.

Contemplating the mantra as a single form within the mental intellect, one should, by means of exhalation (*recaka*), place the Person— the living soul, the Lord— into the jar. One should then fashion his body starting from the principle of time (*kāla-tattva*).

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Kalā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jñānabindu, the lord of the principle of Kalā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to him who brings about the manifestation of the agency of this self as the lordship of Kalā; perform, perform! (Sixth line) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Vidya. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the principle of Vidya, the knower of the meaning of the Vedas.

Oṃ hāṃ! To the Lord of the Principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva), who performs the fulfillment of transformations—namas! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to the Principle of Passion (rāgatattva)! (Second time) Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to Kāmadeva, the Lord of the Principle of Passion!

Oṃ hāṃ! To the lordship of the principle of passion, which effects the fulfillment of attachment to sense objects—*kurukuru*, homage! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ! To the lordship of the principle of primordial nature, which effects awakening—*kurukuru*, homage! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ!...

Salutation to the Buddha, the lord of the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to him who brings about the awakening of this [being] to the state of being the lord of the principle of intellect; perform, perform! (Third line) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of ego (*ahaṃkāratattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ahaṃkṛti, the lord of the principle of ego.

Oṃ hāṃ, perform the act of self-identification as the lordship of the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra-tattva); homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of mind (manas-tattva)! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Candra, the lord of the principle of mind! Oṃ hāṃ, [perform] the act of self-identification as the lordship of this principle of mind...
Perform, perform conceptualization and discursive thought; homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of hearing (*śrotratattva*).

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Tridaśa, the lord of the principle of hearing. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to him who performs the grasping of sound as the sovereignty over the principle of hearing. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of touch (*tvaktattva*).

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu, the lord of the principle of the skin. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to him who makes this [skin] the perceiver of touch through its lordship over the principle of the skin; perform, perform! (Sixth line) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the eye. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Arka, the lord of the principle of the eye. Oṃ hāṃ...
Obeisance to the eye, which performs the grasping of form; obeisance to the element of the eye. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the element of the tongue.
(7th line) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa, the lord of the element of the tongue. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the state of being the lord of the element of the tongue of this [deity].
rasagrāhakaṃ kurukuru namaḥ | oṃ hāṃ ghrāṇatattvāya namaḥ | oṃ hāṃ ghrāṇatattvādhipāya aśvinībhyāṃ namaḥ || (second time)

Oṃ hāṃ! To the lordship of the nose-element, make it the grasper of fragrance, kurukuru, namaḥ! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to the speech-element! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to Agni, the lord of the speech-element! Oṃ hāṃ! To the lordship of the speech-element of this [being], perform the emission of speech, kurukuru, namaḥ! (Second line)

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of the hand (*pāṇi-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Indra, the lord of the element of the hand (*pāṇi-tattvādhipa*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to you who cause this [element] to grasp objects as its lordship; perform, perform! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of the foot (*pāda-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ... (third line).

Salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the element of the feet. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to you, the lord of the element of the feet; grant me the enthusiasm for movement, grant it, salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the element of the anus. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mitra, the lord of the element of the anus. Oṃ hāṃ... (fourth line)

Oṃ hāṃ! Perform, perform the sovereignty over the element of excretion; homage! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to the element of the generative organ. Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to Ānanda, the lord of the element of the generative organ. Oṃ hāṃ! Perform, perform the bliss that is the sovereignty over this element of the generative organ; homage! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to the element of sound. (Fifth line)

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the subtle resonance, the sovereign of the principle of sound. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to you who effect the filling of space, the sovereignty of the principle of sound; perform, perform [this]! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of touch. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the most powerful one, the sovereign of the principle of touch. (Sixth line)

Oṃ hāṃ! To the lordship of the element of touch, perform the filling of wind, perform it, homage! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to the element of form! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to Bhānumat, the lord of the element of form! Oṃ hāṃ!
To the lordship of the element of form, perform the filling of fire, perform it, homage!

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of taste (*rasatattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the principle of taste, the Water-giver (*jalada*). Oṃ hāṃ, perform, perform the filling with water for the sovereignty of the principle of taste; homage. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of smell (*gandhatattva*). Oṃ hāṃ... (second line).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the limb of smell, the presiding deity of the principle of smell.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to you who are the lord of the principle of smell; O Earth, perform the filling, perform the filling! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of space. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva, the presiding deity of the principle of space. Oṃ hāṃ...
O you who grant space through the sovereignty of the element of ether, perform, perform [this]! Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of wind.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśvara, the lord of the element of wind. Oṃ hāṃ, the manifestation of his sovereignty over the element of wind.
kurukuru namaḥ | (4th line) oṃ hāṃ tejastattvāya namaḥ | oṃ hāṃ tejastattvādhipāya rudrāya namaḥ | oṃ hāṃ tejastattvādhipatvam asya pākam |

*Kurukuru namaḥ*. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the water element (*āpastattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the presiding lord of the water element. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to you who perform the grasping of the sovereignty over the water element; *kurukuru namaḥ*. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the earth element (*pṛthivītattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the presiding lord of the earth element.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to you who perform the upholding of the sovereignty of the Earth (the sixth line); thus one should place [the mantra].
Alternatively, [one may recite]: obeisance to those beginning with Kalā and ending with Kṣiti. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to those beginning with Kalā and ending with Kṣiti.
Salutations to Jñānabindu and the others. Oṃ hāṃ! You who are the lords of the principles (tattvas) from Kalā down to Kṣiti—perform, perform your own function for him; salutations.
Having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) of the principles and so forth, one should perform the placement of the channels (nāḍīs) and the rest as follows.
Emerging from the center of the *kanda* and reaching toward the region of the *kuṇḍalī*,
it is situated like a lotus above the navel in the location of the heart.
