In its center, resting upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*), are the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire.
In the center of that, one should contemplate the Lord by the name "Oṃ Hāṃ Haṃ Haḥ," who is the presiding Īśāna,
possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns.
The Suṣumnā extends from the middle of the big toe up to the aperture of Brahmā.
The iḍā resides in the left nostril-passage, and the piṅgalā in the right;
the gāndhārī is in the right eye, and the hastijihvā in the left.
Pūṣā should be in the right ear, and Nayanasvini in the left ear;
Pūṣā is in the penis, while Kuhunāḍī is situated in the anus;
Śaṅkhinī should be in the center of the navel, and the vital winds, beginning with Prāṇa, are in the mouth.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
Oṃ, salutation to the Suṣumṇā nerve. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the prāṇa-vāyu that flows through the Suṣumṇā, and so forth.
The mantras are: "Or else, [the mantras] are 'Salutation to the twelve channels' and 'Salutation to the ten vital breaths.
(5th line) One should place Kāla and Niyati within Māyā, who is the presiding deity of all. "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Māyā. Oṃ hāṃ.

Salutation to Māyādhipa, the Terrifying One. Oṃ hāṃ! Make him the sole master of the domain of Māyādhipati; perform, perform [this]—salutation. Oṃ hāṃ! Salutation to Niyati. Oṃ hāṃ! Salutation to Niyatyadhipa, the Restrainer.
Oṃ hāṃ! Perform, perform the act of governing over destiny for this one; homage! Oṃ hāṃ! Homage to Kāla! Oṃ hāṃ!
Homage to Kālarudra, the sovereign lord of time! Oṃ hāṃ! Perform, perform the state of being the sovereign lord of time for this one—the state of abiding as infinite time! Homage!

"Salutation! Having offered oblations to and recited [mantras] over the three principles beginning with intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with primordial nature (*prakṛti*), along with the Lord (*īśvara*), together with the embodied and unembodied lords, one should effect the cessation.
Now, as an incidental matter, he extends by analogy the pervasion (*vyāpti*) which serves as the seed for the installation of the door and so forth, to the *liṅga*.
The pervasion of the gates and palaces is declared to be like that of the *liṅga*.
This is easily understood simply by means of the thorough knowledge of the pervasion of the *liṅgas* already mentioned and those yet to be described.
In this regard, for the elders, there is no pinnacle (*aśikhara*).
The method for its installation is as stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:

"At the conclusion of the Śukanāsā [the front porch], having established the body like a lotus within the heart-lotus in the center of the Śuka-prāma, according to the yoga of emanation... (3rd line).
Having performed the placement [of mantras], one should effect protection with the armor and weapon mantras using the *haṃsa* seed-syllable.
Having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the world-sustainers, one should firmly secure that entrance.
Then, having constructed the altar, one should fashion the ear-ornament of *āmalaka* wood.
Therein, one should perform the installation like that of the *Īśakṛt* linga.
There, there is no removal of marks; rather, there is the conceptualization of three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*).
The entry of Brahmā is from above, and the Śakti is as before, with jewels and so forth.

"Without ritual knowledge (*kriyājñāna*), the rest [of the rites], such as the placement of the *tattvas* (*tattvanyāsa*) and so forth, are present in that which possesses the marks. Thus, the installation of the banner (*dhvajasthāpana*) must also be performed there; its characteristics and the method of its consecration have been explained in detail in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*.

Let that very point be determined here: where previously the eightfold or fivefold installation of the principles (tattvas), the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras), the forms (mūrtis), and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvaras) was described, that procedure is referred to as "Pratiṣṭhā. He explains that very same procedure: "There, within the portion belonging to Kavi, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, one should install the three principles in sequence."
In that *liṅga*, which consists of one's own *vidyā* and the auspicious nature of the *ātman* accompanied by the respective lords of the *vidyās*,
[the placement occurs] in the portions of Brahmā and Rudra within the division of Kaviṣṇīśa.

One should install the three principles (*tattva*) consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva—namely, the principle of Ātman, the principle of Vidyā, and the principle of Śiva—in their respective order, accompanied by their individual lords of knowledge (*vidyādhipa*). By the word "Vidyā," a mantra is meant;
the meaning is that one should install them with those respective mantras at the conclusion of the *sparśahoma*.

In that context, the *ātmatattva* consists of the twenty-four principles beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*); the *vidyātattva* consists of the seven principles beginning with passion (*rāga*); and the *śivatattva* consists of the five principles of *vidyā*. Regarding the lords of these principles, he says:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are indeed the lords of the three principles within the *liṅga*. Here, the word "*liṅga*" [refers to the body]. (Second line)
The term *piṇḍikā* is also an elliptical expression for both stones.
As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"The installation of the stone at the base of the *liṅga* consists of nine divisions."

The placement of the embodied [deities] and the lords of the embodiments, accompanied by the principles (tattvas) and the lords of the principles, consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara; these three are indeed the lords of the principles within the liṅga.
Thus, the triad of principles is proclaimed as being named Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.

Having thus described the principles (*tattva*) and their lords (*tattveśvara*), he speaks of the forms (*mūrti*) and the lords of the forms (*mūrtyeśvara*): "Either eight or five form-protectors are fixed; the lords of the forms are eight or five, being fixed according to the qualification (*adhikāra*) of those seeking liberation or enjoyment. (4th line) They are determined in accordance with the specific qualification of those known as seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) or seekers of worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*).
In that regard, concerning the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), he describes the eightfold forms and the Lord of Forms (*mūrtīśvara*):
"Earth, fire, the sacrificer, the sun, water, wind, the moon, and space—
these are the eight forms which should be installed in each section."
The meaning is: "in the previously [mentioned] places divided into three sections.
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhava, Īśāna, Mahādeva, and Bhīma—these are the guardians of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrtipāḥ).

The word *padaccheda* (in the sixth line) is itself the explanation of this. It should be understood that the sequence of the forms (*mūrti*) follows the very order of the forms. Thus it is regarding the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*). Having stated the arrangement of the forms and the lords of the forms, he speaks concerning the seeker of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), and that desire for enjoyment pertains to the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*).
And likewise on the path of both the pure and the impure (line 7).

Regarding that, first he speaks concerning the desire for enjoyment on the path of purity: "On the path of purity, from Śuddhavidyā down to Śakti, for the seeker who desires enjoyment, Ananta and the others are the guardians of the forms during the Pratiṣṭhā [initiation]."

In that which is thus described—the path of the pure way (*śuddhādhvan*)—which begins with the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*) and ends with the principle of the Primordial Power (*ādi-śakti-tattva*); for the seeker who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), namely the practitioner desiring the enjoyment of the supreme powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, when the rite of installation is being performed—that is to say, when the installation of the Śiva-liṅga is being carried out—[the result is] fame and the removal of sin. This is the ellipsis to be supplied.

"Kantādyāḥ" [refers to] Kantā and the others. "Mūrtayas tu" means the forms previously mentioned, such as Kṣmā, Vani, and so forth; this is the meaning of the words. The ellipsis is that they are to be placed in each section.

Regarding the sound that consists of both the pure and the impure, [the Lord] spoke for the sake of one who desires to enjoy [the fruits of] the extremely pure and the impure, beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Vāmā. Within that sound, which is of a nature both pure and impure—that is, whose essential form is both pure and impure—the Rudras who are the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipā*), such as Aṅguṣṭhamātraka and the others, are to be known. [This sound] begins with the principle of Puruṣa and extends up to the principle of Māyā. Within that [sound], which is of the nature of water, there exists this essence of both purity and impurity.

The phrase "of one desiring sound" (*dhvanibubhukṣoḥ*) implies [one] who seeks the enjoyment devoid of the *parā-aiśvarya* (supreme powers) such as *aṇimā* and so forth. The phrase "the *mūrtipas* beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra" implies that they are to be understood as those who are to be worshipped and upon whom [mantras] are to be installed. (Fifth Lime) He indicates those very ones, beginning with Ananta, as follows: "And Ananta likewise..."

And Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetraka, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, and Śrīkhaṇḍa (or Śrīkaṇṭha), together with Śikhaṇḍin—this is the remainder [of the list]. Now, for one who desires enjoyment on the pure and impure paths, he says: from Puruṣa up to Māyā.
In the resonance (*dhvani*) consisting of both pure and impure aspects, the Rudras such as Aṅguṣṭhamātraka and others are not to be understood as the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipā*).
[This applies] to that [system] in which the *puruṣatattva* is primary, according to the doctrine of the *māyātattva*. In that [system] in which the *māyātattva* is primary...

[The powers] Vṛddhā, Ātmā, and Aśuddhātmikā [reside] in those whose nature is pure-impure; [they belong] to one who desires sound (*dhvani*) and seeks the enjoyment devoid of the supreme *aṇimā* and other [siddhis]—this is the ellipsis. The *mūrtipās* such as Aṅguṣṭhamātraka and others [are mentioned in the second line].
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is that they are to be known, worshipped, and installed; he points them out as follows.

Having thus described the Lords of Sound and Knowledge (*dhvanividyeśas*) who possess both pure and impure forms— namely Aṅguṣṭhamātra, Bhuvaneśa, Īśāna, Ekapiṅgala, Udbhava, Bhava, and the highly resplendent Vāmadeva— the author now speaks of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*) belonging to the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*).

On the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), which begins with the principle of earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*) and ends with the principle of primordial matter (*pradhāna-tattva*), there are established the forms of the hundred Rudras—eight [of whom] are the lords of the ten directions and so forth. This refers to that impure path, described as such because it has the earth-principle as its beginning and the primordial-matter-principle as its end; it is the object for one who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*).
The remainder:
among the hundred Rudras, those who abide in the *nivṛtti-kalā* are the lords of the worlds (*bhuvanādhipas*), numbering ten in each direction.

Among those numbering one hundred, excluding the lords of the ten directions and so forth, as well as the two lords of the upward direction, it is among the eight lords of the directions alone that the presiding deities of their respective arrays (vyūha-patis) are established; that is to say, they are determined to be the very guardians of the forms (mūrti-pās). (6th line)

Now he points out those very [deities]: Kapālīśa, Agnirudra, Yāmya, the one named Nairṛti, Bala, Śīghra, Nidhīśa, and Vidyādhipati as the eighth. He speaks of the domain of worldly desire (*aihika-bubhukṣā*):
the skin, Indra, and the others are the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*).

They are considered well-known as Bhairavas in certain minor rites. In some cases, for the sake of attaining a son and other such desires, the world-protectors such as Indra and others are to be worshipped as lords of vidyās; and they...
(f35a, first line)
They are indeed well-known. In certain minor rites, such as killing (*māraṇa*) or driving away (*uccāṭana*), the Bhairavas themselves are to be worshipped as the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*).
To the question "Who are they?", he says: Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava. (Second line)

Kapālibhīṣaṇa and Saṃhāra are the eight Bhairavas. Here too, since only the forms (mūrti) and their guardians (mūrtipa) have been mentioned, the forms themselves were already described previously. Having thus explained the alternative regarding the forms in the eight-fold system starting with Earth, [the text now addresses] the five-fold system (line 3).

He states the distinction: "The five forms are the maiden, earth, water, fire, wind, and space; these are the five forms [of Śiva] in the *liṅga*, beginning with Brahmā. Having thus explained in a general manner regarding both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), [he speaks] for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*)... [4th line].
He says that there is also a distinction of objects: "For the seeker of liberation, however, the forms beginning with Nivṛtti reside in the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā];
Sadyojāta and the others reside in the Liṅga; those five are its lords. This is indeed explained by the words themselves. Thus is the principle regarding the forms and their lords in the Liṅga.

Having thus stated [the procedure] for the pedestal-stone (*pīṭhaśilā*) as well, by indicating "and so forth" (*ityādi*), he speaks of the distinction. In this way, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the pedestal-stone is to be performed after having been stated;
the meaning is that it is likewise for the *liṅga*. As for the distinctions and non-distinctions, he will speak of them [in the sixth line].

This is the remainder [of the verse]. He first states that very method for one who desires liberation: "Action, knowledge, and likewise will are considered the presiding deities of the three principles. The power of action (kriyā-śakti), the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and the power of will (icchā-śakti) are the presiding deities of the three principles.
They are known as Ātman, Vidya, and Śiva, the presiding deities of the triad of principles.

[They] are considered [to be such], with "in sequence" being the ellipsis. Having thus described the distinction between the Lords of the Principles (tattveśvara), he states the distinction between the Lords of the Embodiments (mūrtīśvara):
Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, and these [others], Balotkaṭā, Dhātrī, and Bahvī, are considered the Lords of the Embodiments in the sphere of the Pīṭhas.

Regarding the domain of the *pīṭhas* and so forth—that is, in relation to the *pīṭhas* and the *śilās*—the eight powers beginning with Dhārikā are considered to be the presiding deities (*mūrtyadhīśvaras*) of the forms (*mūrtis*). Now, for the sake of one who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), he says: "In the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), [the presiding deities] of the forms on the *pīṭhas* and so forth are Ananta and the others."

Thus they should be [present] when the female seats have come down; for the practitioner desiring enjoyment, when [the deity] has entered into the installation within the field, she has come under the control of the female seats. This means that they are indeed Ananta and the others, [specifically] the powers of the Lords of Knowledge such as Ananta. "The sovereigns of the forms are to be worshipped" (third line).

The remainder [is as follows]. Having thus stated the division according to the eightfold scheme, he speaks also regarding the fivefold scheme: "Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñāna, and Icchā—these are intended as the lords of the five forms (mūrtīśas) on the pedestal and so forth. On the pedestal and the like, specifically on the pedestal-stone (piṭhaśilā), the five powers beginning with Vāmā are the lords of the forms; they are to be worshipped—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Now, regarding the pedestal-stone...

Since the forthcoming installation of images applies equally to both the *liṅga* and the image, [the author] first states the specific distinction regarding the two types of stone for the fierce forms (*ugramūrti*).
(5th line)

The worship of Ugrā is now being described. By the word "Ugrā," rites such as *abhicāra* (malevolent magic) and other minor operations (*kṣudrakarma*) are indicated for those whose forms are intent upon the worship of Ugrā; that is to say, [the worship] employed for such rites. This is what is being stated regarding their pedestals and foundation stones.
The remaining part [of the instruction] is that the placement of the Mūrti and Mūrtīśas is according to the sequence of the eight wings (*pakṣa*). He states that very sequence:
"Tama, Moha, Kṣaya, Nidrā, Mṛtyu, Māyā, Bhaya, and Ajvara; on the wing [are] Tama, Moha, Aghora, Ati, Para, Jvara, and Amata.
(7th line)

Thus, having described the fierce worship (*ugrārcanā*) of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the pedestal-stone (*pīṭhaśilā*), as well as the distinction between the form (*mūrti*) and the lord of the form (*mūrtīśa*),

[the author now explains] first, upon the pedestal-stones of the *liṅga*, the sequential order of the distinctions according to which the five forms— beginning with Earth and ending with Space— pervade the reality (*tattva*) of each respective element.
He says that one should meditate according to the sequence about to be described:

"One should contemplate the deity as distinct within the five forms, as well as in the linga, the pedestal, and the stone, through the successive attainment and pervasion of the principles (tattvas)."
Thus, it is easily understood according to the sequence of divisions that will be described.
He states that very sequence:
Fire ends with Rāga; Water ends with Kāla;
and the Linga of Space ends with Īśvara and Śiva.
Earth is the form of the Earth element; "ending with Rāga" means extending up to the principle (tattva) of Rāga; and Water is the form of the Water element.

The fire-forms extend to the end of *kāla*, reaching as far as the *kāla-tattva*; the forms of *vidyā* extend to the end of *vidyā*, reaching as far as the *vidyā-tattva*; the forms of *vāyu* extend up to *Īśvara*; the space-linga extends up to *Śiva*;
and the earth (*kṣmā*) extends up to *rāga*, reaching as far as the *rāga-tattva*.
Water is the embodiment of water, extending up to Kāla and culminating in the principle of Kāla; fire is the embodiment of fire, extending up to Vidyā and culminating in the principle of Vidyā;
wind is the embodiment of wind, extending up to Īśvara; and space is the embodiment of space, extending up to Śiva.

The meaning is that one should contemplate the sequence of pervasion up to the principle of Śiva, [visualizing] the Linga as the Linga itself. Now he speaks of the seat (pīṭha): "Up to the Puruṣa, ending with the Earth-element; Water ends with Māyā; Fire goes up to Śuddhavidyā;
and Wind ends with Śakti. (6th line)
The Celestial Seat (*vyomapiṭhaka*). Now, he explains the sequence of pervasion (*vyāptikrama*) within the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*): Earth ends with the elements; Water ends with the word;
Fire ends with the organs of action; Wind ends with the organs of cognition; and Space resides in the abode ending with the intellect.
[Thus] the Linga is pervaded in the stone, the Brahma-stone.
This is easily understood through the method of explanation.

In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, the manner of performing the deposition of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*) is as follows: "The Guru, having stood at the region of the feet, should begin the deposition of the principles and so forth."
One should install the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) in the *liṅga* with the syllable *sauṃ* and the *dhruva-mantra*.
Having relied upon the thread of power (*śaktisūtra*), one should commence the installation of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*). Om.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Soma, the lord of the Śiva-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śakti-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dharmī, the lord of the Śakti-tattva. Thus, in the portion of Rudra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Sadāśiva-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lord of the Sadāśiva-tattva. (Second line)

Salutation to Ajeśa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Īśvara (Īśvaratattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the four-faced one, the presiding lord of the principle of Īśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyātattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kalyāṇa, the presiding lord of the principle of Pure Knowledge. (Third Line)

Thus, for the portion of Viṣṇu: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Māyā (māyā-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣāṇa, the presiding deity of the principle of Māyā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Kalā (kalā-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ketudhvaja, the presiding deity of the principle of Kalā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Kāla (kāla-tattva). (4th line)
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the principle of Time, whose face is like a cresting flame. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of Necessity.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the principle of Necessity, the Great Banner.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of Ignorance. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the principle of Ignorance. (5th line)

Salutation to Meghanihrāda. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rāgatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Pallava, the lord of Rāgatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Puruṣatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of Puruṣatattva. Oṃ hāṃ... (6th line).

Salutation to the principle of Prakṛti. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Pitāmaha, the presiding deity of the principle of Prakṛti. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Buddhi. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Buddha, the presiding deity of the principle of Buddhi.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Ahaṅkāra. Oṃ hāṃ... (7th line)

Salutation to Ahaṅkṛti, the lord of the principle of ego (ahaṅkāra-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of mind (manas-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Saṅkalpa, the lord of the principle of mind. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of hearing (śrotra-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vyomadharā, the lord of the principle of hearing.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the skin. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the principle of the skin, the All-Limbed One. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the eye. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the principle of the eye, the Illuminator.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the tongue. Oṃ hāṃ... (second line)

Homage to Mahāvaktra, the lord of the principle of the tongue. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the nose. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vilumbaka, the lord of the principle of the nose. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dundubhi, the lord of the principle of speech. Oṃ hāṃ... (third line).

Homage to the principle of the hand (*pāṇi-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the presiding deity of the principle of the hand, Sāmagāna, and to the mind (*manas*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the foot (*pāda-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the presiding deity of the principle of the foot, Saṅkramaṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the anus (*pāyu-tattva*).

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the element of excretion, Tūrṇakṛt. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of the generative organ. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the element of the generative organ, Ghanānanda. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of sound. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the element of sound.
Salutation to Sūkṣmanāda.

(5th line) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of touch; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the most powerful lord of the principle of touch; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of form; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhānumat, the lord of the principle of form; Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to the principle of taste (*rasa-tattva*).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the giver of water, the lord of the principle of taste. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of smell (*gandha-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to the limb of smell, the presiding deity of the element of smell. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the element of space. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sūkṣma, the presiding deity of the element of space. (7th line) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the element of air. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mātariśvan, the presiding deity of the element of air. Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to the principle of fire (*tejastattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the principle of fire, the master of splendors. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of water (*aptattva*).

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Water, the Master of the Water Element. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Earth Element. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha, the Lord of the Earth Element. Thus, in the Brahma-section. Alternatively: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the thirty-six principles.

*Namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Rudras, the lords of the thirty-six principles; thus one should install [them] simultaneously.* Then, relying on the eightfold division, regarding the manner of pervasion of the eight forms beginning with Earth, [this applies] even to the *liṅga*, the pedestal, and the stone.
He states that each [form] is to be meditated upon individually:

"In the eightfold system, however, the forms beginning with Earth and ending with Īśāna are located from the East to the Northeast. He also explains another system for ease of understanding: "In the fivefold system, they are situated in the West, South, Southeast, East, and Northeast. (4th line)

This is the meaning: the Earth is presided over by the Brahma Sadyojāta; in the western direction, Water is presided over by the Brahma Vāmadeva; in the southern direction, Wind is presided over by the Brahma Tatpuruṣa; in the eastern direction, Space is presided over by the Brahma Īśāna; and likewise in the northeast.
"One should place" means one should contemplate.

Thus, on the linga, the pedestal, and the stone, they are contemplated through the placement (*nyāsa*) of the principles (*tattva*), the lords of the principles (*tattveśvara*), the forms (*mūrti*), and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*). (6th line)

Having described the procedure [for the installation of a temple], he extends it by analogy to images as well, stating: "In this very same way, it should be understood that this entire sequence applies even to images. However, he shows the distinction: "In the case of images, such as those in the dancing posture (*nṛttamūrti*) and so forth, the placement of the three principles (*tattvatrayanyāsa*) extends up to the knees, the shanks, and the head."

This same entire procedure is to be observed even for images of Śiva. He states that there is a specific distinction regarding the deposition of the three principles (*tattva*): "But... [referring to] up to the knees, ears, and head.
The *ātmatattva* extends to the knees, and the *vidyātattva* extends to the ears.

One should thus assign the Śiva-tattva ending at the head; the meaning is that everything else is as before. However, in the case of an image—as with a liṅga—the conceptualization of three principles (*tattvas*) is performed: the one called Ātman extends down to the knees, the one called Vidyā is situated up to the palate, and the one called Śiva extends to the top of the head.

One should perform [the rite] as before with the syllable *ṣaṃ*. Thus [it is said]. Now, he describes the difference in procedure for the placement [of mantras] during the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of both the door and the temple (*prāsāda*).
Regarding the door: the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti-tattva*) resides in the three-fold divisions (*trikhaṇḍaka*) of the door-posts (*duṃbara-śākhā*).
Therein, having divided the door into three sections, [one should place... situated below... (3rd line).

The meaning is that one should contemplate the *vidyā-tattva* as pervading the lower section from the *baramāsa* [downwards], and the *śiva-tattva* as pervading the upper section starting from the *uduṃbara*, and thus install them. Now, having installed the *ātma-tattva* within the body— its range extending as far as *māyā*— one should then install the *vidyā-tattva* as far as the *deśa*.
Having placed the Śiva-tattva, ending with Śakti, upon the two branches of the *uduṃbara* tree;
likewise, the temple (*prāsāda*) is also threefold...
there, one should contemplate the Ātma-tattva as extending to the knees, the Vidya-tattva to the neck, and the Śikhara-tattva to the crest.
One should perform the placement (*vinyaset*). Now, he states the specific details regarding the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of Gaurī and the others:

[one should place] the principles of Sadāśiva, which are established in the middle of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) fashioned by the aforementioned *nyāsa* for the installation of the *mukhaliṅga* and other types.

The thirty-six principles (*tattva*) of the path of reality (*tattvādhvan*), beginning with Earth and so forth, which were previously described as eightfold and fivefold for Mūrti, Mūrtīśvara, and the others—

by means of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the text] establishes the logical basis for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of those three principles and the powers of knowledge and action (*jñāna-śakti* and *kriyā-śakti*) through their mutual existence.

In the absence of mutual integration among all [the factors], there is an absence of reciprocal connection; therefore, the seed is that which acts by coming together independently for both enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).
The seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*), the names, and the coarse mantras (*sthūlamantra*)— which are the forms of the respective deities to be meditated upon as will be described—

are presented according to their actual state, since they do not enter the intellect in the absence of knowledge of their forms; [this applies to] the other terms such as Earth and so forth that will be described [in the fourth line].

Having meditated upon the sequence of the end of the duration and having correctly ascended [to that state], one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) even upon images and all types of *liṅgas* and pedestals (*piṇḍikā*), because they are pervaded [by it] from the very beginning among those things to be consecrated;
this is so in the absence of knowledge regarding these [matters].

Since that very [kind of] assignment is impossible, it is indicated by this that the teacher’s thorough knowledge of the principles (*tattva*) of the established doctrines (*siddhānta*) of the four quarters of the Śiva-āgamas is also the seed of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). Now,
for the sake of thoroughly knowing [the deities] as they actually exist, [there follows the description] of the embodied and unembodied lords (*mūrtimūrtīśa*), and so forth.

He states their positions: Earth is established in the state of water; the principles beginning with *tanmātra* are situated in their respective domains; the two, Soma and Sūrya, are stationed in the forms of the *śabdatanmātra*; above those two is the one called Dharma; and Śarva is established in the *gandhatanmātra*.
Stability resides in form (rūpa).
I am Ugra, the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati), whose sphere is the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). Rudra is to be understood as being right there, while Bhava resides in the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra).
Īśāna is situated in the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra) as Mahādeva, and Bhīma resides in the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra).
"Abiding in the lords of the forms. Its meaning is as follows:

(second line) "Established in earth and water"—that is, the fourfold group beginning with water [abides] in its respective domain, such as water in fire, fire in air, air in space, and so forth; by this, the relationship of cause and effect among earth and the other elements is shown through the relation of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*).
(Third line) It should also be understood as follows:
above the subtle element of sound, at the forefront of the subtle form of space, the moon and the sun are situated.

And above those two, the moon and the sun, is that which is called Dharma. Dharma is the form of the sacrifice known as Jyotiṣṭoma and others, established by tradition; he who possesses that [form] is the sacrificer. Through metaphorical identification (*upacāra*), there is non-difference between the action and the agent; thus, it is the sacrificer himself [who is meant].
He is established as the nature of *dharmatva*. By this, the establishment of the eight forms (*mūrti*) has also been stated.
Now, the establishment of the lords of the forms, beginning with Śarva, among the [objects] such as smell (*gandha*) and so forth, is for the sake of clarity.
Having thus described the state of the lords of the forms for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), [the author now describes] the lords of the forms for those seeking enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*).

He describes the station of the Vidyeśvaras: "The Vidyeśvaras are to be known as established in the principle of Vidyā. The Vidyeśvaras are Ananta and the others. By this, the Bhairavas such as Asitāṅga and the rest, who perform minor activities, are also implied; they too reside in that very place.
Because of the systematic arrangement.
Now, relying on the fivefold system, he says: "From the earth up to the slaughter of a human being, Acyuta extends from Brahmā down to Māyā;
Rudra extends from the earth up to Vidyā; Īśvara extends from the earth up to Vidyā."

The [principles] beginning with Sādākhya and ending with Nāda constitute Śakti; this Śakti, whose nature consists of will, knowledge, and action, begins with Dhārikā and ends with Ka, and extends from the element Earth up to the Śiva-tattva—this is the meaning of "is situated. Thus it is.

It has been stated that the Śivaliṅga is essentially the abode (*ālaya*), because it is the ground for the placement of all the paths (*adhvan*). Now, in order to indicate that those belonging to other systems (*siddhāntetara*) who occupy the stations of the *samaya* are merely partial aspects of this [Liṅga] and nothing else, he describes their abiding within the lower principles.

The ten incarnate forms of Viṣṇu abide in the element of earth (*pṛthvī-tattva*). The "ten incarnate forms" refers to the various manifestations of the incarnations beginning with the Fish (*matsya*).
Abiding in the element of earth, they are within the sphere of the Bhūtas, Hṛt, Buddhi, Ahaṃkāra, the group of *gaṇas*, Puṃs, Vidyeśvara, and Mitrā and the others.
The twelve beginning with Keśava, the twelve beginning with Tryambaka, the twelve beginning with Mitra,
the twelve beginning with Keśava-Īśa (or Keśaveśa), and the twelve beginning with Tryambaka.

Thus, the twelve [limbs] are also threefold; the meaning is that they are situated respectively within the twelve principles— earth and the others— namely, the five elements, the principle of mind (*manas*), the principle of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the qualities (*guṇa*), the principle of the person (*puruṣa*), the principle of knowledge (*vidyā*), and the principle of the Lord (*īśvara*).
Vighnarāja resides in Sādākhyā; likewise, the Goddess Sarasvatī is there.
Nandī and the others reside in Śuddhavidyā; Lakṣmī resides within the sphere of Īśvara; [and] Prakṛti [is the locus].

The Jains are established in Saṃskṛta; the Śākyas are established in the Buddha; those who know the Pañcarātra are established in Puruṣa; and the Sūryas are established in Śiva. Indeed, the Apsarases, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras [are likewise established in their respective deities].
The spirits, vetālas, and ḍākinīs; the planets, lunar mansions, and zodiac signs; the oceans, field-protectors (kṣetrapālas), and so forth; the sages, Brahmā, and the lords of the directions;
as well as those born from a womb, from an egg, and from moisture—these are to be known as abiding in the upper realm (ūrdhvatatva).
For others as well, wherever they are established among the principles (tattvas),

that very place where the ritual placement (nyāsa) ends is indeed their swift destination. This applies to those beginning with Vighnarāja and ending with the Lords of the Directions, according to their respective locations in the consecrations (pratiṣṭhā).

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed upon whichever specific principles (*tattva*) among those extending to the ultimate reality (*tattvaparyanta*) are situated; for each of those respective locations is itself the supreme state (*paramapada*). For this very reason, every initiate (*samayin*) considers the very station prescribed in their own particular scripture to be the highest of all. But if this is so—

Since each of those respective scriptures was composed by their corresponding great personages (*mahāpuruṣa*), [one might object: "If there is doubt, then even the Śaiva scripture would be stained by the suspicion of lacking authority. If this is argued, we reply: No.
Because this [scripture] was composed by Śiva, who is endowed with qualities such as omniscience, it does not fall within the scope of such doubts or suspicions. Nor...
It should be stated that because Saṅghabhadra is also omniscient, the treatises composed by him would likewise be authoritative;
for the omniscience of Kapila and others is also established through the practice of yoga and other means. Let both of them be omniscient—what loss is there to us?
If it is argued that there is a loss [of consistency], we say no; for they have composed mutually contradictory scriptures. As it has been said:
"If Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not?"
"If both are omniscient, how can there be a difference of opinion between them?"— therefore,
the mere thorough knowledge of that reality alone is the ultimate limit for others, consisting solely of that very reality.
Since the Śiva-śāstra was composed by the omniscient Supreme Śiva, its primary essence is the reality of Śiva from the very beginning.

It has been established that this alone is the supreme state and that initiation (*dīkṣā*) is indeed the means for attaining that state. Furthermore, it was stated previously in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The abode of the Form (*mūrti*) shall be one, stainless, and facing in all directions."
"Immovable, all-pervading, peaceful, and devoid of [all] marks (liṅga)—
for those who remain unconquered by themselves, their form [is realized] through initiation."

"And they do not see those places of liberation, O Six-faced One. Thus it is said that, in the context of the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*), the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Mūrtīśvara and Tatveśvara principles must be performed. Regarding that: (second line)

Since the placement (*nyāsa*) is thus easily accomplished once one is familiar with the meditation on their essential forms (*svarūpa*), he describes their limbs, ornaments, and so forth according to their distinct prior forms, beginning with "four-faced" and so on. Furthermore, the sequence of these [limbs] is not intended here, as that has already been stated previously.
First, he describes the form of Earth: (3rd line)
She has four faces and eight arms, wears yellow garments, is established in action,
possesses a gentle form, and is surrounded by oceans, rivers, and serpents.
He spoke concerning the Water-form:
"Varuṇa has been surpassed; he who is joined with the dolphin-bannered [vehicle] has departed.
His very self possesses the nature of four arms, and he is adorned with all ornaments."

He describes the form of Fire: "The consumer of oblations, mounted upon a ram, with blazing rays and a spear in his hand, has a mouth shaped like a sacrificial pit and possesses a radiant, flaming luster. (5th line)
He describes the form of Vāyu: four-armed, four-faced, smoke-colored, and of great strength;
seated on a deer, holding a goad, pervasive, with knitted brows, and ever-moving.
They say his form is space;

he has four arms and four faces, holding a trident, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a skull-cup in his hands, while grasping a conch and a *khaṭvāṅga*; his radiance is like that of the sky, a jasmine flower, the moon, and snow.
He describes the form of Soma:
"Soma is gentle, seated upon a celestial vehicle, holding a mace and a conch, bestowing boons,
resembling a jewel of universal form, and endowed with the nectar of the sixteen digits."

He spoke concerning the form of Sūrya: "The Sun is mounted upon a chariot drawn by horses; he wears armor and earrings, possesses a banner and a crown, holds a lotus in his hand, is adorned [with ornaments], and has Aruṇa as his charioteer.
He spoke concerning the form of the Sacrificer (*yajamāna*): [f41b, first line]
The sacrificer is proclaimed to have black horns, a black turban, and to be accompanied by Rāma and Sumeghali,
with his limbs smeared with fresh butter.
This is for the sake of clarity. Now, indicating that Śarva and the others possess forms just like the Mūrti-Īśvaras and the Vidyeśvaras, he says:
(second line) "Endowed with the qualities of the world-protectors and characterized by corresponding weapons."
The guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), beginning with Śarva, are considered to possess bodies as described by the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa). This is indeed a self-explanatory statement.

Having thus explained the position regarding the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti-pakṣa), he now states, in the case of the five forms (pañcamūrti-pakṣa), those which consist of the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti.
Nivṛtti is proclaimed to have the appearance of molten gold, adorned with four arms and a moon, and holding a vajra, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus.
The image of Pratiṣṭhākalāmūrti resembles pure crystal; she has two faces and four arms,
holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, and is adorned with the jewels of consecration.
Vidyā is the embodiment of the Kalās; she is red in color, with a moon upon her matted hair, three faces, and four arms;
holding a spear, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, Vidyā is radiant like a blazing fire.
Śāntikalāmūrti has four faces and four arms; she is black in color and possesses great strength.
Holding a banner, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, Śānti wears a serpent as her sacred thread.
The form of Śāntyatītākalā is like pure crystal; she has five faces and four arms,
holding a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, and she bestows boons as Śāntyatītā.
Now he describes the forms of the five Brahmas as embodied deities:
Sadyojāta wears the attire of a youth, has three eyes, bears the full crescent moon upon his crest,
is adorned with water-born earrings, and has eyes resembling white lotuses.
"Āpyaḥ" means the lord of the waters, Varuṇa, whose face is directed toward the quarter [of the west].
"Sadyaḥ" refers to Sadyojāta; this is a case of mentioning a part of a name to denote the whole, as in the example "Bhīma" for Bhīmasena.
The left [hand] is a woman; his face is gentle, adorned with the ornaments of a beloved;
he is decorated with matted hair and the moon, stout, and possesses eyes like the petals of a beautiful lotus.
Vāma is Vāmadeva; he is gentle (saumya), facing the direction of the Moon (Soma);
his eyebrows, beard, and moustache are tawny, and his eyes are red; he is adorned with a trident and the crescent moon; and he has three eyes, resembling a fresh rain cloud.
His face was disciplined by the Lord of Death; the word "non-terrible" (aghorah) is to be understood as the remainder [of the description].
Richly adorned with high feet, beard, and attire, he was purifying and endowed with youth.
His face was decorated, and he was embellished with serpents, skulls, and matted locks.

The *puruṣa* [face] is remembered as being red in color, with matted hair and a crescent moon; because it is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) consisting of "serpents and skulls" (*vyālaka-pāla-jaṭa*), it takes the neuter gender. Therein, the *īśāna* [face] is situated facing upward, with its eyes looking up and down toward the cardinal directions.
Adorned with earrings, three-eyed, and remembered as wearing a crown and the young moon;
he is equipped with a hand-drum, a serpent-eye, a garland, and a blue lotus;
and in his right hands, he holds a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a spear, a trident, a boon-granting gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness.
Now, regarding the subject of those who desire enjoyment, he speaks by resorting to the eightfold perspective:
"The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) have four faces and ten arms like Hara;
they all have the crescent moon upon their crests, are seated upon lotuses, and bear various weapons."
Holding swords, shields, bows, arrows, water-pots, and rosaries,

they are endowed with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and have tridents and lotuses in their hands. Now, he describes the eight forms beginning with Śakra, each with half a verse:
Śakra, the thousand-eyed wielder of the thunderbolt, mounted upon his elephant and surrounded by the Maruts,
was encircled by garlands of flames, holding a spear in his hand and seated upon a goat outside.
Yama has bloodshot eyes, carries a staff, and is fearsome; he rides upon a buffalo.
Mounted on a corpse, with a gaping mouth, he wields a sword and a club, and possesses fierce eyes.

Varuṇa has a white complexion, stands upon a fish, holds a noose in his hand, sits upon a deer, and wields a goad; Vāyu possesses a body composed of the four elements. Vaiśravaṇa is said to have a large, circular belly and carries a mace.
Resembling a jasmine flower, the moon, or snow, seated upon a bull, wearing a crescent moon,
equipped with the weapons mentioned by Vidyeśa, and enveloped in a single matted lock (ekajaṭā), [he is Śiva]. Now, [the author] describes the forms of the Lords of the Causes, beginning with Brahmā:
Brahmā has four faces, is adorned with four staff-like arms,

is equipped with a garland, a staff, a rosary, and a sacrificial ladle, wears a crown, and has a swan as his vehicle. Viṣṇu has four arms, wears a garland, and holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, seated upon Garuḍa, five-faced,
fifteen-eyed, ten-armed, and adorned with the moon;
Rudra is indeed seated upon a bull, wearing a sacred thread, and as pure as a jasmine flower or the moon.
Eight-armed, four-faced, with the luster of crystal and three eyes,
he should be known as the Lord Dhruva, wearing a serpent as his sacred thread; the god is pure as the jasmine and the moon, his great body consisting of the five mantras.
The ten-armed, serene-faced, five-faced Sadāśiva—
now [the author] states the essential natures of the principles (tattvas) of the Śiva-knowledge:
[He is] four-armed, four-faced, and seated upon a square lotus.
This reality of the Self indeed abides with the luster of molten gold;
resembling a sapphire, it is blue, eight-cornered, and endowed with eight arms.
It has a single face and a serene countenance; this is proclaimed as the reality of Knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*).
The Śiva-tattva is indeed remembered as being like a jasmine flower, the moon, or snow; it is circular, containing all the paths (adhvan), five-faced, and four-armed.
Thus, having described the forms of the Mūrtis and Mūrtīśvaras which constitute the limbs of the Pratiṣṭhā [tattva].
He states that when the place and time—which serve as constituent factors of the installation—are employed [correctly], they bestow the desired fruit; otherwise, there is a fault:
"Sacrifices performed only in one's own country and at one's own time yield the desired fruit; in another country and at another time, they become causes of the undesired. (4th line)

The specific regions and specific times have been demonstrated by us in the *Śaivakālaviveka*; they should be understood from that very source. The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "performed in another region and at another time. These alone are the causes of failure for the sacrifice. (5th line)

[They] produce what is undesirable. Now, one might object: since the body is like a bubble on water, and because merit such as consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) must be performed at the very moment of remembering and practicing the *Śivadharmas*, otherwise even a transference [of merit] might not occur, why is it said that it "must be performed"?
To this, he says: "Therefore, of the consecration... (line 6).

One should perform the rites known as *deśāpātana* and *kālāpātana*. Therefore, for the very reasons stated above, one should perform the rituals called *deśāpātana* and *kālāpātana* during the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). He explains the procedure for that as follows: "In the south-eastern direction, [one should perform] *deśāpātana*, and in the eastern direction, *kālāpātana*. (43b, first line)
One should worship:

having invoked the deity in one's own *svāṣṭaka*, and having placed him outside the region; in one's own *svāṣṭaka*—that is, in the middle of the five *aṣṭakas*—in one's own *svāṣṭaka*, meaning in one's own desired group of eight; having invoked the deity situated outside, that is, the presiding lord of each respective world. Having invoked...
Having established that the location is not more than that [specified],
he states its very external nature: one should worship the place in the south-eastern direction near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the sacrificial hall,
and the time in the eastern direction.
The distinction lies in the two mandalas.
(Third line) He states the times and places: from one's own twelve [periods], the *kṛtyā* belongs to one's own [mandala];

from the enemy [mandala] possessing its own [periods], [the periods] are obtained on earth as five; and from the eight [periods] of the Lord of the Immortals (*amareśa*) in sequence, starting from the *kṛtyā*—that is, from the domain of the rite of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*). (Fourth line)

[Line: From one's own [cycle] of twelve, from the fivefold group of twelve years; that is to say, beginning from one's own year, the year of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). "The times are to be honored"—this is the ellipsis; they have been obtained on earth.

Those situated in the stages of the foundation and establishment upon the surface of the earth—the group of eight beginning with Pañcamareśa—have already been described previously during the occasion of defining the paths (*adhvan*). Those [eight] are indeed the five regions. As for time, however, it begins with *prabhava*.

"By means of the twelve-fold sequence. This refers to the time beginning with the *prabhava* year and so forth. "By means of the twelve-fold sequence": starting from the *pratiṣṭhā* year, through the application of the twelve-fold sequence, even within the sixty-year cycle there are five divisions; this is the meaning. He now states the presiding deities of the aforementioned places and times.
In these five [faces],
there are, in order, the causal lords beginning with Pañcabrahman; others also reside within the limits of their pervasion, being joined to those respective locations and so forth.

Within these five groups of eight and also within the five groups of twelve, Brahmā and the other Lords of Causes—namely those previously mentioned as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—are to be worshipped in sequence; this is the remainder [of the statement]. This is due to their pervasive presence.

By virtue of their connection with the Lord who is the cause of that [place], others as well are joined to this specific location and so forth. The sense is that, in the worship of the deity of this place, one who is connected to this very place and time must necessarily perform the ritual acts known as "establishing the place" (*deśāpādana*) and "establishing the time" (*kālāpādana*). Now...

Since the deity of the site (*vāstudevatā*) is also introduced in connection with the topic of location, he says: "Now, in connection with location, the deities of the site are seen" (line 4). Furthermore, they are the deities of the site for the purpose of the worship of the site (*vāstupūjā*), as they constitute a constituent part of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). In that regard:
First, he assigns the sixty-four deities of the *vāstu* (site-plan) known as the "frog-step" (*maṇḍūkapada*). [They are:
Brahmā, Īśa, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendra, Arka, Satya, Bhṛśa, Antarikṣa, Saptarci, Pūṣan, and the one named Avitatha.
Graha, Kṣata, Pretapati, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgaka, Mṛga;
Pitṛ, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Pracetas;
Asura, Śoṣa, Roga, Vāyu, Nāga, and then Mukhyaka.
Bhallāṭa, Soma, Moha, Diti, and Aditi;
Marīci, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Dharādhara; Āpa, Apavatsa, Savitṛ, Sāvitra, Indra, and Indrajittama.
Rudra, Rudradāsa, Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā,
the sinful Rākṣasī, Skanda, Aryaman, Jambhakas, and Balipiṇḍa—
these are declared to be the fifty-three [Grahas], and thus they conclude.
Among these, regarding the common cause of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-sāmānya*), it has been explained that [the deity] is prone to falling away.
For example, he lies upon the ground with his face turned downward like a house-demon (*vāstu-nara*);
because of his ferocity and his capacity to cause fear, he should be worshipped by those who desire auspicious results.
The head is situated in the northeast square, and the feet are joined with the southwest square. In the center, at the Brahma-square, is the navel; this limb follows all the squares.
[He is] four-armed, with matted hair and a crown, holding a water-pot and an akṣa-bead rosary.
Placing the left hand above the knee with the palm facing upward,
one should worship the golden-hued Lotus-born [Brahmā] with offerings such as perfumes and the like,
and then cast a bali-offering consisting of pure food mixed with curd, clarified butter, and jaggery.
All [the deities], endowed with four arms and holding swords and shields,
with palms joined in reverence, having been meditated upon as stationed in their respective places,
[should be worshipped] with their respective name-mantras preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*.

Having recited [the mantra] and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should cast the aforementioned bali-oblation. The meditation for each [deity] has been stated individually in our *Śivālayanirmāṇadīpikā*; let that be consulted there. It has not been written here for fear of excessive length in the text. Thus...
In order to specify the respective locations for the fifty-three deities beginning with Brahmā, he describes the method for drawing the sixty-four-square *vāstu* diagram:
"The square below" [is the first]; the remainder [of the sentence] is that it is called the *vāstu*-square immediately following [the central one].

There are eighteen lines facing east and north, which constitute the channels (nāḍikās). The two beams (vaṃśas) are situated at the two corners, and there are eight cords (rajjus), each consisting of eighteen squares.
Thus, by way of incidental explanation, the sacred site (vāstu) consists of sixty-four squares.
Nine lines facing east and nine lines facing north;
these two together form eighteen lines, which are the *nāḍikās*.
They take the form of a grid, with both [ends] reaching the corners.

Starting from Kṛnnī and ending at Vāyavya, or starting from Aiśāna and ending at Nairṛta, there are eight ropes known as the "dog's teeth" (*śauvaśākhya*); the remainder [of the description] is that they are situated at the corners. Among them, each set of four ropes consists of eight and six squares within three squares each; and that—(4th line).
The meaning is that there are two lines per square in the third row, four lines per square in the second row, and six lines per square in the first row; thus it occurs for each direction.
And so it is stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
The characteristics and names of the channels, cords, and bamboos have also been stated;
for example, [the mandala] is endowed with sixty-four squares and accompanied by eighteen lines.
It is provided with two ear-threads, adorned with eight cords,
endowed with twelve vital points (marmans), and accompanied by the fires, the elements, and the gods.
I shall describe separately the characteristics of their positions known as the "frogs.
The lines of the site, which are its channels, run either toward the east or toward the north.
[The deities of these lines are] Lakṣmī, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Supriyā, Vimalā, and Śivā.
Subhagā, Samanī, Corvinā, and Ḍyā emerge facing east;

Dhānyā, Prāṇā, Viśālā, Sthirā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Niśā, Vijayā, and Vibhavā are known as the gentle-faced [goddesses] facing north. Durjayā and Dūrdhvarā are situated diagonally and upwards, along the two bamboo-frames (vaṃśa).

Those two, situated in the mother’s and father’s houses, when pierced, cause the destruction of that lineage. Four [lines] situated in a triangle are "encircled by a rope," and likewise four are "two-footed.
Of those four which are "six-footed," I shall state their names according to tradition.
Kīrṇa and Kilanirajju are for binding the feet and the ankles; Saṃvartā and Vivartā are for the junctions of the knees and elbows;
and likewise, Janani is for the regions of the heart, the private parts, and the belly.
The cords used in the binding of the site are to be known as "bird-yakṣīs.
I shall now describe the twelve vital points (*marmāṇi*) situated upon the limbs of the site:
the confluence of all the channels, the great vital point, the lotus, and the plow.

The trident, the swastika, the thunderbolt, the great swastika-casket, the triple-junction, the wrist-bond, and likewise the perfectly pure station—these are the twelve vital points (*marmas*). One should abandon devotion to those who have attained [worldly] success. The characteristics of these are also stated in that very same place.
In the sixty-four-square site known as Maṇḍūkapada, it should be thus; the extraction [of the squares] should occur according to the method described.
Now, he says that the squares are being stated for the purpose of worshipping the fifty-three deities previously mentioned.
The fifty-three deities are indicated here in their proper sequence. Here, in the *maṇḍūkapada* [style], they are indicated (*uddiśyante*),
which means they are applied (*viniyujyante*) and specified (*nirdiśyante*), because they have already been indicated previously.

In the center, on the four-footed [altar], is Brahmā, the six-legged bee of the rays of light (*marīci*). The meaning is that he is to be worshipped there because "Brahmā has four feet" (*brahma-catvāri-padāni asya*), thus forming the term *catuṣpada*. (Second line) Within that very space, in the eastern direction, is the six-legged bee of the rays of light. In the third rite, there are two feet; in the second rite...

The meaning is that it consists of six words, namely the four quarters [of the verse] and so forth. He states that of those two very injunctions, there are two words located in the southeast corner (the third line), [beginning with] *adhi*...; furthermore, *svitā* refers to that which is situated in the southeast corner, and the word *sāvitra* is for the sake of clarifying the meaning even further.
By the northern path from the eastern and southeastern directions [one proceeds] to the southern and northwestern;
from the western and northwestern to the northern and northeastern.
Āvivastvan is in the six squares of the south; Indra is at the foot of the Rakṣas square. Below that is Indrajaya; and in the northern and friendly [squares]...

The six squares [beginning] from the wind-corner are for Rudra; below that are the Rudradās. The meaning is clear. Now, on the outer path (*bāhyavīthī*), starting from the southern half of the square of Īśāna and extending to its northern half, in thirty-two squares:

He states that thirty-two squares are to be worshipped: "Beginning from the half-square of Īśāna and ending at the half-square of Aiśāna, [proceeding] from the edge in the direction starting with Īśāna until the end, there are thirty-two [squares] in clockwise order. The meaning is: by way of a clockwise sequence.

Among the fifty-three deities previously mentioned, he states that there are forty-five deities residing within the *vāstu* [site-plan]: "Thus, forty-five deities reside within the body of the *vāstu*. Now, as for the remaining eight deities..."

He says, "situated outside the site" (*vāstubahisthitaṃ*). Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the evil Rākṣasī—these four are situated at the spikes in the corners starting from the northeast (*īśāna*). In the north, there are four [deities] such as Balipiñchā and others, located outside.
The meaning is that they are to be worshipped in the four directions starting from the east within the circles in sequence.
And likewise, in the *Aṃśumatī*: "Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and Pāparākṣasī."

One should offer the *bali* in the center of the trident, from the southeast (Āgneya) to the northeast (Īśa). Likewise, Skanda, Aryaman, Jambha, and Balipiñcaka—[these] one should offer as *bali* in the four directions starting from the east, in the middle of the circle. Having thus described the "frog-step" (*maṇḍūkapada*), [the rite continues].
He spoke of the state of supreme rest. In the diagram of eighty-one squares, the rule for the center of the site consists of nine squares.
[The deities] are Marīci, Vivasvat, Mitra, Bhūdhara, Āpa, Apavatsa, Savitṛ, Sāvitra, Indra, and Tajjaya.
"Rudra and his servant [Śiva] are known to have two feet, while others are remembered as having one foot.
Since the meaning is clear, it need not be further explained.
Likewise, in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī* (6th line):

When the field has been divided into eight squares by the lines of the cross, there are eight squares for the *dharma* and *adharma* [lines], two for the *vaṃśa* [pillars], and two for the *koṇa* [corners]. Within the space between them, four squares are for the *vidhi*, and two squares at the intermediate directions are for the *samaya*. Six parts starting from the east belong to the *śruti* squares, while four squares are for the *tridaśa*, and two squares situated outside are for the *pada*.
Likewise, in the other corners, there are the desired squares; outside, the others starting from Īśa (northeast). In the eighty-one-square [mandala], the lotus-born [Brahmā] occupies nine squares;
there are eight lines situated in six and three [rows]; the Marīci and Mukha [deities] occupy two squares each; and the others are situated in eight squares.

Having thus stated the matter as it was proposed, he concludes by demonstrating its utility: "The teachers, having grasped these two seeds—initiation and establishment—strive for their completion at the proper time through diligent effort. (3rd line)
"Skilled in the established tenets of the four pillars of the Śiva-āgamas" is the address. "You" is the understood subject of the instruction. In the Vīra-tantra it is said:
"He by whom the place [of practice] is pointed out is known as a *deśika* (guide)."
Initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*): these two have been thus described.

Having properly grasped the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) from the mouth of the Guru, and having thoroughly mastered them at the time of initiation and the time of consecration, you should strive for their accomplishment and their application. Perform this; it is indeed your own undertaking.

The sense is that this [work] has the supreme purpose [of attaining liberation]. Now, since the enduring purpose of composing this treatise is fame (*kīrti*), for that reason, he first mentions the names of his patron kings and then reveals his own name, followed by the number of verses that set forth the summarized meaning.
"Under the pretext of [writing] a work," he says;
thus, the venerable Somabhūbhṛt, the teacher, extracted from hundreds of scriptures those two seeds which were suddenly perceived together at that time.
The one named Śrī Varuṇa; the teacher Śrī Somabhūbhṛt and the initiations of King Śrī Somabhūpāla.

(7th line) The one named Śrī Varuṇa. At various times when those respective tasks were to be performed, [all] from one place—in a single work alone. The sense is that this was done so that [the teachings] might be perceived at a glance, because the Āgamas are extremely extensive. (f47b, 1st line)

The meaning is that, in the manner described, those two seed-syllables (*bīja*) were set forth from the *Āgamas* beginning with the *Kāmika*, by means of two hundred works consisting of two hundred verses. Thus he brought them forth.
He did not bring them forth while awake; here, for the learned, there is the manifestation of the protection of the ground (*bhūmi*) upon which he himself rests. (2nd)

This is for the purpose of indicating that it should be accomplished by kings and scholars who are well-known; furthermore, its designation as "Varuṇa" should be understood as referring to the casting of flowers and so forth upon the petal of the western direction (varuṇadik) within the initiation mandala (dīkṣāmaṇḍala). As it has been said:
In this commentary on the *Pūjāstava*,
one should follow the method therein. This "Eye," composed by me according to my own understanding through the *Varuṇapaddhati*,
should always be opened with compassion by the virtuous.

[Thus ends the second chapter, the Section on the Seed-syllables of Installation, in the Vilocana commentary on the Varuṇapaddhati composed by Nigamajñānadeva, son of Vāmadeva, a resident of Śrīmad-Yāghrapura.]
Salutations to Tripurasundarī!
May the virtuous forgive the offense committed by my hand:
the errors of dots, misplaced visargas, rules of euphonic combination, the sequence of syllables, and the division of words, all arising from the haste of my hand and born of lack of understanding.
May the virtuous person, having considered this, grant forgiveness;
[this work] is offered to Vedapurīśvara together with the illustrious Bālāmbā.
